ra-ts025.x:
In 1973, the sociologist Mark Granovetter published a paper with a surprising title: "The Strength of Weak Ties." He distinguished between strong ties, such as close friends and family members, and weak ties, such as acquaintances, former classmates, and colleagues seen only occasionally. Common sense suggests that the people closest to us are the most helpful, but Granovetter found that weak ties often matter more in one important area: finding a job.

When he interviewed professional workers who had recently changed jobs, many reported that they had learned about their new position through someone they saw only rarely. Granovetter explained this pattern by looking at how social networks are structured. Close friends tend to know one another and move in the same circles, so they usually share the same information. Acquaintances, by contrast, belong to other groups and can act as bridges to news that a person's inner circle has never heard.

The idea has since been applied far beyond the job market. Researchers have used it to study how innovations spread, how rumors travel, and how online platforms connect strangers. The lesson is not that close relationships are unimportant, but that a wide network of loose connections gives people access to a more varied flow of information.

ra-ts026.x:
Around the year 1700, Bartolomeo Cristofori, an instrument maker working for the Medici family in Florence, built a keyboard instrument unlike any before it. The most popular keyboard of the time, the harpsichord, produced its sound when small quills plucked the strings. Because a pluck sounds much the same however hard the key is pressed, a harpsichord player could not easily make individual notes louder or softer. Cristofori's invention replaced the quills with small hammers covered in leather that struck the strings and then immediately fell back, allowing them to vibrate freely.

This mechanism gave players direct control over volume: a gentle touch produced a soft tone, and a firm one produced a loud tone. The instrument's original Italian name described this ability, calling it a harpsichord "with soft and loud." Over time, the name was shortened to pianoforte, and eventually simply to piano.

The early piano spread slowly, but by the late eighteenth century composers such as Mozart were writing music that depended on its expressive range. During the nineteenth century, builders added cast-iron frames, which could withstand far greater string tension than wooden ones. The result was a louder, richer sound that could fill large concert halls.

ra-ts027.x:
Water alone is poor at removing grease from skin or dishes, because oil and water do not mix. Soap solves this problem through the unusual shape of its molecules. Each soap molecule has two very different ends. One end, often called the head, carries an electric charge and is attracted to water. The other end, a long tail made of carbon and hydrogen atoms, is repelled by water but mixes easily with oils and fats.

When soapy water meets a greasy surface, the tails push into the grease while the heads remain in the surrounding water. Eventually, the molecules surround tiny droplets of oil, forming clusters called micelles, with the tails pointing inward and the heads facing out. Because the outside of each micelle is attracted to water, the trapped grease can be rinsed away.

Soap is traditionally made by heating fats or oils with a strong alkali such as lye, a process known as saponification. However, ordinary soap has a weakness. In hard water, which contains dissolved calcium and magnesium, soap reacts with these minerals to form a sticky scum that clings to sinks and bathtubs. For this reason, many modern cleaning products use synthetic detergents, which work in a similar way but are far less affected by hard water.

ra-ts028.x:
Most of the open ocean is surprisingly poor in life. Sunlight reaches only the upper layer of water, where tiny drifting algae called phytoplankton carry out photosynthesis, but this sunlit layer often lacks nutrients such as nitrates and phosphates. These substances tend to accumulate in deeper, darker water, where the remains of dead organisms sink and decompose.

Along certain coastlines, however, nature brings the two together. When steady winds blow parallel to the shore, the rotation of the Earth causes surface water to move away from the coast. Cold water from below rises to replace it, a process known as upwelling. Carrying nutrients into the sunlit zone, this rising water fertilizes enormous blooms of phytoplankton, which feed small fish and, in turn, seabirds, seals, and larger fish. Although upwelling regions cover only a small fraction of the ocean's surface, they support a remarkably large share of the world's fish catch. The waters off Peru, for example, hold one of the largest fisheries on Earth, based on a small fish called the anchoveta.

Upwelling depends on the wind, so it can weaken. During El Niño events, the winds off South America slacken, warm surface water spreads toward the coast, and fish populations can fall sharply.

ra-ts029.x:
In the early twentieth century, the anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski spent long periods living among the people of the Trobriand Islands, off the eastern coast of New Guinea. His detailed account, published in 1922, described an exchange system known as the kula, which linked communities on a ring of islands spread across hundreds of kilometers of sea.

The kula involved only two main kinds of objects: necklaces of red shell and armbands of white shell. Remarkably, these valuables traveled in opposite directions. Necklaces moved around the ring clockwise, while armbands moved counterclockwise, so that a man who received a necklace from one partner would eventually give it to a partner on another island. No one kept the objects permanently. Their value came from their history, including the famous people who had once held them, and from the reputation a person gained by passing them on generously.

To outsiders, sailing long distances in canoes to exchange ornaments that could not be eaten or used might seem wasteful. Malinowski argued otherwise. The kula created lasting partnerships between distant communities, and ordinary trade in food, pottery, and tools took place alongside the ceremonial exchanges. His study helped convince anthropologists that economic behavior cannot always be explained by practical need alone.

ra-ts030.t: Ebenezer Howard and the Garden City
ra-ts030.x:
By the late nineteenth century, industrial cities in Britain were crowded, smoky, and often unhealthy, yet people kept moving to them for work. The countryside offered fresh air and space but few jobs. In 1898, a London clerk named Ebenezer Howard proposed a way to combine the advantages of both. In his book, he illustrated the choice with a diagram of three magnets: the town, the country, and a third option he called "town-country," which would attract people with the best features of each.

Howard's garden city would be planned from the start for a limited population of roughly thirty thousand people. Homes, factories, parks, and shops would be arranged in rings around a central garden, and the whole town would be surrounded by a permanent belt of farmland. Once a city reached its planned size, growth would continue by founding a new garden city nearby rather than by expanding outward. The land would be owned collectively, so that rising land values would benefit residents rather than private landlords.

Two towns, Letchworth and Welwyn Garden City, were built in England according to his principles. Howard's broader influence was even greater: the idea of a protected green belt around a city became a standard planning tool in many countries.

ra-ts031.x:
It might seem natural to assume that a child's brain develops simply by adding more and more connections. In fact, the story is more surprising. During the first years of life, neurons form synapses, the junctions through which they communicate, at an extraordinary rate. In some regions of the brain, a young child has far more synapses than an adult. Development then proceeds partly by elimination: over the following years, many of these connections are removed in a process known as synaptic pruning.

Pruning is not random. Connections that are used often tend to be strengthened and kept, while those that are rarely active are more likely to be eliminated, a principle sometimes summarized as "use it or lose it." Immune cells in the brain called microglia appear to help by engulfing unwanted synapses. The result is a network that is less crowded but more efficient, shaped by the experiences a child actually has.

The timing of pruning differs from region to region. Areas involved in vision and hearing are refined relatively early, while the prefrontal cortex, which supports planning and self-control, continues to be pruned into the teenage years and beyond. This late refinement may help explain why judgment continues to mature well after childhood.

ra-ts032.x:
The potato was first domesticated thousands of years ago in the Andes Mountains of South America, where farmers developed many varieties suited to cold, high-altitude fields. Spanish travelers encountered it in the sixteenth century, and by the 1570s it had reached Spain. From there, it spread slowly across Europe.

At first, many Europeans were suspicious of the new crop. The potato belongs to the same plant family as several poisonous species, and its green leaves and sprouts do contain toxic compounds. Some people regarded it as food fit only for animals. Rulers and reformers who recognized its value had to work hard to change these attitudes. In the eighteenth century, Frederick the Great of Prussia encouraged peasants to plant potatoes, and in France the pharmacist Antoine-Augustin Parmentier promoted the crop through public demonstrations and dinners.

Their efforts were eventually rewarded. Potatoes grew well in cool, damp climates and produced far more calories from a single field than wheat or rye did. They could also be stored in the ground or in cellars for months. Some historians argue that the spread of the potato contributed significantly to the rapid population growth that much of Europe experienced in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

ra-ts033.x:
Ordinary steel, which is mostly iron with a small amount of carbon, is strong and inexpensive, but it has a familiar weakness. When exposed to oxygen and moisture, its iron slowly turns into rust, a reddish-brown iron oxide. Rust is loose and flaky, so it tends to break away from the surface, exposing fresh metal underneath to further attack. Left unprotected, a steel object can eventually be eaten through.

Stainless steel avoids this fate not by keeping oxygen away entirely but by putting oxygen to work. It contains at least about 10.5 percent chromium, and chromium reacts with oxygen even more readily than iron does. The reaction produces an extremely thin layer of chromium oxide, only a few billionths of a meter thick and completely transparent. Unlike rust, this film clings tightly to the metal and seals it off from air and water. Even more usefully, if the surface is scratched, the exposed chromium quickly reacts with oxygen in the air and the protective layer forms again.

The protection is not perfect. Salt can break down the film in places, which is why steel used near the sea often contains extra elements, such as molybdenum, that help the layer resist chloride. Still, the principle explains why stainless steel has become a standard material for kitchen sinks, cutlery, and surgical tools.

ra-ts034.x:
When a honeybee worker discovers a rich patch of flowers, she does not keep the find to herself. Back at the hive, she performs a series of movements on the vertical surface of the honeycomb that other workers can interpret. The Austrian biologist Karl von Frisch spent decades studying these movements, and his work earned him a share of the Nobel Prize in 1973.

The most informative movement is the waggle dance. The dancing bee runs forward in a straight line while shaking her abdomen from side to side, then circles back and repeats the run. The direction of the straight run encodes the direction of the food. Because the hive is dark, the bee uses gravity as a reference: a run straight up the comb means "fly toward the sun," while a run angled 40 degrees to the right of vertical means "fly 40 degrees to the right of the sun." The length of each waggle run signals distance, with longer runs indicating more distant flowers.

Other workers follow the dancer closely, sensing her movements through contact and vibrations, and they also pick up the scent of the flowers on her body. They then leave the hive and search the indicated area. Few animals other than humans are known to communicate the location of distant objects in such an abstract, symbolic way.

ra-ts035.x:
In 1899, the American economist and sociologist Thorstein Veblen published The Theory of the Leisure Class, a sharp and often ironic study of wealthy society. Veblen noticed that the rich frequently bought things not because those things were especially useful but because buying them was visible to others. He called this behavior "conspicuous consumption." A handmade silver spoon, he observed, stirs food no better than a cheap one; its real function is to show that its owner can afford to spend money without practical need.

According to Veblen, such spending is a way of competing for social standing. In a large, anonymous society, people cannot easily judge one another's wealth directly, so they rely on visible signs: fine clothing, large houses, elaborate entertainment. Veblen also argued that this habit does not stay at the top. Each social class tends to imitate the one above it, so the standards set by the rich gradually shape what ordinary families consider necessary.

The idea remains influential. Economists use the term "Veblen goods" for luxury items whose desirability can actually increase as their price rises, since a high price is part of what makes them impressive. Later sociologists have added that status can also be displayed through taste, education, and knowledge, not only through money.

ra-ts036.x:
For centuries, much of the music sung in medieval Europe was passed on by memory. Singers spent years learning a large repertoire of chants by ear from more experienced singers. By the ninth century, scribes had begun writing small marks called neumes above the words of a text. Neumes showed whether a melody rose or fell, but they did not indicate exact pitches, so they served mainly as reminders for singers who already knew the tune.

In the early eleventh century, an Italian monk and teacher named Guido of Arezzo helped solve this problem. Building on earlier experiments, he is often credited with popularizing a system of horizontal lines on which notes could be placed, with each line and each space representing a specific pitch. Some versions even used colored lines to mark particular notes. For the first time, a trained singer could look at an unfamiliar melody and sing it correctly without having heard it before.

Guido also developed a teaching method that linked each step of the scale to a syllable, taken from the opening of each line of a well-known hymn. These syllables are the ancestors of the do, re, mi still used in classrooms today. Guido claimed that his methods allowed singers to learn in a short time what had once taken many years.

ra-ts037.x:
The appealing crust on a loaf of bread, the dark surface of a seared steak, and the rich aroma of roasted coffee all share a chemical origin. Each results largely from the Maillard reaction, named after the French chemist Louis-Camille Maillard, who described it in the early twentieth century. The reaction occurs when amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, react with certain sugars under heat. It is not a single reaction but a complex network of them, producing hundreds of different compounds that contribute flavor, aroma, and a brown color.

Temperature is critical. The Maillard reaction proceeds slowly at ordinary cooking temperatures and speeds up dramatically at around 140 degrees Celsius and above. This explains why boiled or steamed foods rarely brown: as long as water is present, the surface of the food cannot rise much above 100 degrees, the boiling point of water. Cooks who want a good crust therefore pat meat dry before searing it and avoid crowding a pan, which traps steam.

The Maillard reaction is often confused with caramelization, which also produces brown color and complex flavors. However, caramelization involves sugars alone breaking down and generally requires even higher temperatures. In many foods, the two processes take place together.

ra-ts038.x:
Winds drive most of the currents near the ocean's surface, but the deep ocean moves for a different reason. Its circulation depends on density, which is controlled by two properties of seawater: temperature and salt content. Cold water is denser than warm water, and salty water is denser than fresh water. Scientists therefore call this pattern thermohaline circulation, from the Greek words for heat and salt.

The process begins mainly in a few polar regions, such as the North Atlantic near Greenland and the waters around Antarctica. There, surface water loses heat to the frigid air. In addition, when sea ice forms, it leaves much of its salt behind in the surrounding water. The resulting water is both cold and salty, and therefore dense enough to sink thousands of meters to the sea floor. From there it spreads slowly through the ocean basins, gradually rising toward the surface elsewhere before eventually returning to the polar regions. A single parcel of water may take on the order of a thousand years to complete the journey.

This vast system, sometimes called the global conveyor belt, carries heat, oxygen, and nutrients around the planet. Some scientists are studying whether large amounts of fresh water from melting ice could slow the sinking that keeps the conveyor moving.

ra-ts039.x:
People rarely think about how far apart they stand during a conversation, yet most follow unspoken rules. In the 1960s, the American anthropologist Edward T. Hall introduced the term proxemics for the study of how humans use space in communication. Hall argued that the distance people keep from one another is not random but is shaped by their relationship and by their culture.

Based largely on observations of middle-class Americans, Hall described four zones. Intimate distance, less than about half a meter, is usually reserved for close family members and partners. Personal distance, extending to a little over a meter, is typical of conversations between friends. Social distance, from about one to three and a half meters, is common in business and among acquaintances, while public distance, beyond that, is used for speeches and lectures. When someone enters a zone that the situation does not call for, people often feel uncomfortable and step back, sometimes without realizing it.

Hall emphasized that the exact boundaries differ across cultures. A distance that seems warm and friendly in one society may feel intrusive in another, and the reverse. Such differences, he suggested, can lead to misunderstandings when people from different backgrounds meet, since each side may misread the other's behavior as cold or pushy.

ra-ts040.x:
For a long time, making tools was considered one of the abilities that set humans apart from other animals. Observations of chimpanzees weakened that idea, and a bird from a group of Pacific islands has challenged it further. The New Caledonian crow not only uses tools but also manufactures them with remarkable skill.

In the wild, these crows feed partly on insect larvae hidden inside dead wood. To reach them, a crow may strip leaves from a twig and shape the end into a small hook, or cut a narrow strip with a tapered, saw-toothed edge from the tough leaves of the pandanus plant. The bird then pokes the tool into a hole and draws out its prey. Interestingly, the shapes of pandanus tools differ from one part of the islands to another, which has led some researchers to suggest that the designs are passed on socially, much like local traditions.

Laboratory studies have added to the picture. Young crows raised without adults still begin to handle twigs and probe with them, suggesting that the basic behavior is partly inborn. Yet juveniles in the wild spend a long period near their parents, watching them work, which likely helps them refine their technique. In one well-known experiment, a captive crow bent a straight piece of wire into a hook to lift a small bucket of food from a tube.

ra-ts041.t: Jane Jacobs and the Life of the Street
ra-ts041.x:
For much of the mid-twentieth century, influential planners treated the dense, untidy city street as a problem to be solved. Inspired in part by Le Corbusier's vision of towers set in open parkland, they favored separating residential, commercial, and industrial uses, replacing tangled blocks with large superblocks, and clearing older districts wholesale in the name of renewal. In 1961, Jane Jacobs, a writer with no formal training in planning, challenged this orthodoxy in The Death and Life of Great American Cities.

Jacobs's central claim was that urban vitality arises not from grand design but from intricate, overlapping activity. Streets lined with shops, homes, and workplaces draw people at different hours, and their continual presence provides what she called "eyes on the street": an informal, largely unconscious surveillance that, in her view, keeps streets safe more effectively than policing alone. Short blocks, a mix of old and new buildings, and sufficient density, she argued, all sustain this diversity.

Her ideas are now so widely accepted that it is easy to forget how radical they once seemed. Yet some critics contend that Jacobs underestimated economic pressures: the very neighborhoods she celebrated have often become so desirable that rising rents displace the residents and small businesses that made them lively.

ra-ts042.x:
Few questions in neuroscience have been debated as persistently as whether particular mental abilities reside in particular parts of the brain. In the early nineteenth century, phrenologists claimed that traits such as kindness or ambition could be read from bumps on the skull. Their method was soon discredited, but the underlying intuition, that the brain is divided into specialized regions, proved more durable.

Strong support came in 1861, when the French physician Paul Broca studied a patient who could understand speech but produce almost none. Examining the patient's brain later, Broca found damage concentrated in a region of the left frontal lobe, now called Broca's area. A little over a decade later, Carl Wernicke described patients with the opposite pattern: fluent but largely meaningless speech, associated with damage farther back in the left hemisphere.

Not everyone was persuaded. In the twentieth century, the psychologist Karl Lashley trained rats to run mazes and then removed different portions of their cortex. He reported that the rats' performance depended less on which area was removed than on how much, leading him to propose that memory is distributed broadly across the cortex. Most neuroscientists today adopt a position between these extremes, regarding complex functions as emerging from networks of specialized regions working together.

ra-ts043.x:
The shift from foraging to farming, which began independently in several regions roughly ten thousand years ago, is often portrayed as an obvious improvement. Skeletal evidence complicates that picture. Early farming populations in a number of regions appear to have been shorter on average than their foraging predecessors and to have suffered more from tooth decay and nutritional deficiencies. If agriculture initially made life harder, why did people adopt it?

One early answer, proposed by the archaeologist V. Gordon Childe, held that a drying climate at the end of the last Ice Age forced people, plants, and animals into close contact around scarce sources of water, encouraging domestication. Later research, however, found little evidence of such widespread drying. Other scholars emphasized demographic pressure: as populations grew, foragers may have been compelled to extract more food from less land, even at the cost of harder work.

A more recent and contested proposal shifts attention from necessity to ambition. According to the feasting hypothesis, individuals seeking prestige cultivated surplus grain to host lavish communal events. Supporters point to monumental sites, such as Göbekli Tepe in present-day Turkey, that appear to have been built by hunter-gatherers, suggesting that large social gatherings may have preceded, rather than followed, settled farming.

ra-ts044.x:
In everyday terms, a windowpane is unmistakably solid: it holds its shape, resists pressure, and shatters when struck. At the level of atoms, however, glass is less easily classified. In a crystalline solid such as quartz, atoms are arranged in a regular pattern that repeats over long distances. In ordinary glass, which is made largely from the same silica, the atoms are locked in place but lack this long-range order, resembling a snapshot of a liquid frozen in time. Materials of this kind are known as amorphous solids.

This structure arises because glass is cooled from a melt too quickly for crystals to form. Rather than solidifying abruptly at a fixed melting point, as ice does, the material grows steadily more viscous over a range of temperatures until it becomes rigid.

Such observations have encouraged a persistent myth: that glass is really a very slow liquid, and that the panes in very old buildings are thicker at the bottom because the glass has flowed downward over the centuries. Calculations suggest otherwise. At room temperature, the viscosity of glass is so enormous that any noticeable flow would take far longer than the age of the universe. The uneven panes are better explained by older manufacturing methods, which rarely produced sheets of uniform thickness.

ra-ts045.x:
In 1928, the sociologists W. I. Thomas and Dorothy Swaine Thomas offered an observation that later became known as the Thomas theorem: if people define situations as real, those situations are real in their consequences. Two decades later, Robert K. Merton built on this insight with the concept of the self-fulfilling prophecy, a false belief that, by shaping behavior, brings about the very outcome it predicts.

Merton's best-known illustration was a bank run. Imagine a bank that is financially sound until a rumor spreads that it is about to collapse. Anxious depositors rush to withdraw their savings, and because no bank keeps all of its deposits as cash, the rush itself can drive the bank into failure. The prediction was initially false; it became true only because people acted on it.

The idea was later applied to education. In a widely publicized study in the 1960s, teachers were told that certain randomly chosen pupils were likely to make unusual intellectual gains, and those pupils reportedly improved more than their classmates. Subsequent researchers, however, criticized the study's methods, and attempts to replicate it have generally found expectation effects that are real but considerably smaller than first claimed. The concept, then, remains valuable, though its power in any given setting should not be assumed.

ra-ts046.x:
Popular accounts of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart often portray him as a composer to whom entire works arrived fully formed, needing only to be copied onto paper. Much of this image rests on a letter, published in 1815, in which Mozart supposedly described hearing whole compositions in his mind at a single moment. Scholars now widely regard the letter as a forgery, and its appeal may say more about the nineteenth century than about Mozart. Romantic writers were drawn to the idea of the artist as a vessel for mysterious inspiration rather than as a skilled craftsman.

The surviving documents tell a more complicated story. Mozart left behind sketches, drafts, and a considerable number of unfinished fragments, some abandoned after many measures. These suggest that he, like other composers, tested ideas, revised them, and sometimes set them aside. Admittedly, his memory and speed were extraordinary, and he could work out a great deal mentally before writing. Yet extraordinary fluency is not the same as effortlessness.

The contrast is often drawn with Beethoven, whose sketchbooks record painstaking struggles over individual themes. That contrast, however, may partly reflect what happened to survive. Beethoven kept his sketches, whereas many of Mozart's working papers were probably lost or discarded, so the evidence itself may exaggerate the difference between them.

ra-ts047.x:
Natural selection, in its simplest form, favors individuals who survive and reproduce. Behavior that helps others at a cost to oneself therefore poses a puzzle, one that troubled Charles Darwin himself when he considered sterile worker insects that labor for the colony but never reproduce. How could a tendency toward self-sacrifice persist if those who display it leave fewer offspring?

In 1964, the biologist W. D. Hamilton proposed an influential answer. Because relatives share many of the same genes, an animal that aids a sibling or cousin can promote copies of its own genes indirectly. Under this theory of kin selection, helping should be most common when the benefit to the recipient, weighted by how closely the two are related, exceeds the cost to the helper. Field studies have offered support: ground squirrels, for instance, are more likely to give risky alarm calls when close relatives are nearby.

Kinship cannot explain everything, however. Vampire bats that fail to find a meal will often receive regurgitated blood from roost-mates, some of which are unrelated. Researchers have found that bats tend to share with individuals that have previously shared with them, a pattern consistent with Robert Trivers's theory of reciprocal altruism, in which help is effectively exchanged over time.

ra-ts048.x:
For much of the twentieth century, a single account dominated the study of how people first reached the Americas. Distinctive stone spear points, first identified near Clovis, New Mexico, were found at sites across North America, many dating to roughly 13,000 years ago. Many archaeologists concluded that the makers of these points were the continent's first inhabitants: hunters who had crossed a land bridge from Siberia and then traveled south through an ice-free corridor that opened between two vast ice sheets in what is now Canada.

This "Clovis first" model began to unravel when excavations at Monte Verde, in southern Chile, revealed evidence of human occupation that by most estimates predated Clovis by more than a thousand years. If people were living near the southern tip of South America so early, they must have entered the Americas earlier still. Moreover, some researchers argue that the inland corridor would not yet have provided enough food and shelter for travelers when those earlier migrations would have needed it.

Attention has therefore turned to an alternative route along the Pacific coast, where people with boats might have moved south while exploiting marine resources. Testing this idea is difficult, however, because sea levels have risen since the end of the last Ice Age, and many early coastal sites now lie underwater.

ra-ts049.x:
For much of the twentieth century, feathers were treated as the defining feature of birds, and their origin was assumed to be bound up with the origin of flight itself. Discoveries in northeastern China since the 1990s have complicated that picture. Fossils preserved in fine volcanic sediments reveal that many small theropod dinosaurs, including species that could not plausibly have flown, bore filament-like or even branched feathers. Feathers, it now appears, predate flight by millions of years.

If feathers did not evolve for flight, their original function remains contested. Some researchers argue that simple filaments served chiefly as insulation, a plausible advantage for small, active animals that may have had elevated metabolic rates. Others point to the elaborate, sometimes patterned plumage of certain species and propose that display, whether to rivals or mates, drove its elaboration. The two hypotheses are not mutually exclusive; a structure that first retained heat could later have been co-opted for signaling.

This reframing has consequences for the long-running debate over how flight arose. The 'ground-up' model holds that running predators gradually gained lift by flapping, whereas the 'trees-down' model envisions gliding from elevated perches. Because feathered limbs were already present in non-flying ancestors, neither scenario now needs to explain the feathers themselves, only how existing structures were repurposed.

ra-ts050.x:
In the 1930s the philosopher Karl Popper proposed that what distinguishes science from other kinds of inquiry is not that its claims can be confirmed but that they can, in principle, be refuted. A genuinely scientific theory, on this view, forbids certain observations; if those observations occur, the theory must be abandoned. Popper contrasted bold, risky predictions with doctrines so flexible that any outcome could be reconciled with them, which he regarded as unfalsifiable and therefore unscientific.

The criterion proved enormously influential, yet historians and philosophers soon questioned whether it describes how scientists actually behave. Thomas Kuhn, writing in the 1960s, observed that researchers working within an established framework rarely discard it when an experiment fails. Instead, they tend to treat anomalous results as puzzles to be solved, attributing them to faulty instruments or overlooked variables. Only when anomalies accumulate does a field undergo what Kuhn called a paradigm shift.

A related objection holds that no theory is ever tested in isolation. Any prediction relies on auxiliary assumptions about equipment and background conditions, so a failed prediction does not by itself reveal which assumption is at fault. Defenders of Popper reply that his criterion was meant as a normative ideal rather than a description: an account of how scientists ought to reason, even if they sometimes do not.

ra-ts051.x:
In the winter of 1636–1637, prices for certain tulip bulbs in the Dutch Republic rose to extraordinary levels before collapsing abruptly in February. The most prized bulbs produced flowers with vivid streaks, a pattern now known to be caused by a virus, and because such bulbs could not be reliably reproduced, they were scarce. For generations the episode served as the archetypal speculative bubble, largely thanks to an 1841 account by the Scottish writer Charles Mackay, who described ruined merchants and a nation gripped by collective folly.

More recent archival research suggests that this portrait is overdrawn. Much of the frenzied trading appears to have involved contracts for future delivery, negotiated in taverns, and many of these agreements were never honored or enforced. Historians who have examined notarial records find little evidence of the widespread bankruptcies Mackay reported, and the broader Dutch economy seems to have continued largely undisturbed.

Some economists go further, contending that early prices for rare varieties reflected rational expectations about a fashionable luxury good, and that only the final weeks of trading were genuinely irrational. Others caution that the surviving records are fragmentary, so any verdict on the participants' motives must remain tentative. What is clearer is that moralizing retellings shaped the episode's reputation as much as the events themselves did.

ra-ts052.x:
When caterpillars chew on a leaf, many plants respond by releasing a blend of volatile organic compounds into the air. Some of these airborne chemicals have a well-documented function: they attract parasitic wasps and other predators that attack the herbivores, so the damaged plant effectively recruits bodyguards. A more controversial question is whether undamaged neighbors also respond to these signals.

Early reports in the 1980s that trees near damaged individuals increased their chemical defenses were met with skepticism, partly because the experiments lacked adequate controls. Since then, better-designed studies on plants such as wild tobacco and sagebrush have found that exposure to a damaged neighbor's volatiles can prime defenses, allowing the receiving plant to respond more quickly when it is later attacked. Such findings lend the phenomenon considerable plausibility, though effects measured in the field are often modest.

Interpretation, however, remains divided. Describing the process as plants 'warning' one another implies that the emitter benefits from alerting competitors, which is difficult to explain in evolutionary terms. Many botanists therefore prefer to say that neighbors eavesdrop on cues released primarily for the emitter's own benefit, perhaps to coordinate defenses among its own distant branches. On this account, the signal is public, but its purpose is private.

ra-ts053.t: The Cloud Problem in Climate Projections
ra-ts053.x:
Estimates of how much the planet will warm in response to rising carbon dioxide depend heavily on feedbacks, processes that amplify or dampen an initial change. Some feedbacks are comparatively well understood. Warmer air holds more water vapor, itself a greenhouse gas, which strengthens warming; melting snow and ice expose darker surfaces that absorb more sunlight. Clouds, by contrast, have long been the largest single source of disagreement among climate models.

The difficulty arises because clouds exert opposing influences. Low, thick clouds reflect incoming sunlight back to space and thus cool the surface, whereas high, thin clouds let much sunlight through while trapping outgoing heat, producing a net warming effect. Whether a warmer world will have more of one type or the other, and at what altitudes and latitudes, is hard to determine, not least because individual clouds are far smaller than the grid cells that global models use to represent the atmosphere. Their behavior must therefore be approximated rather than simulated directly.

In recent years, satellite records and high-resolution simulations have narrowed the range somewhat, and many researchers now judge it likely that clouds, taken as a whole, slightly amplify warming. Nevertheless, the uncertainty has not disappeared, and it continues to account for much of the spread in projections of long-term temperature rise.

ra-ts054.x:
When Warner Bros. released The Jazz Singer in 1927, the film was not the first to use recorded sound, nor did it contain much synchronized dialogue; most of it was silent, with musical accompaniment. Its few sequences of song and speech nonetheless caught the public imagination, and within roughly three years most Hollywood studios had converted to sound production. The speed of the transition is often cited as evidence of audience demand, though some historians stress that studios were also responding to rivals' investments in competing sound technologies.

The change imposed new constraints. Early microphones picked up the whirring of cameras, so cameras were at first enclosed in soundproof booths, which made them difficult to move. Actors had to stay near hidden microphones, and many early sound films consequently appear static compared with the fluid camerawork of late silent cinema. Some critics at the time lamented what they regarded as a step backward for the art form.

These limitations proved temporary. Technicians soon developed quieter cameras and soundproof housings, known as blimps, as well as microphones mounted on movable booms. By the early 1930s, directors had recovered much of their earlier visual freedom, and sound was being used creatively rather than merely recorded.

ra-ts055.t: Learning by Remembering: The Testing Effect
ra-ts055.x:
Tests are usually regarded as tools for measuring what students have learned, but a substantial body of research indicates that they can also change what is learned. In typical experiments, participants study material and then either reread it or attempt to recall it without looking. On an immediate check the two groups often perform similarly, or rereaders do slightly better; after a delay of days or weeks, however, those who practiced retrieval usually remember considerably more. This pattern, known as the testing effect or retrieval practice, has been replicated with word lists, prose passages and classroom content.

Why retrieval should strengthen memory is less settled. One account holds that the effort of searching memory elaborates the original trace, linking it to additional cues that later aid recall. Another proposes that retrieval helps learners reinstate the context in which the material was first studied. Researchers also note that the benefit is larger when the practice is effortful, an instance of what has been called a desirable difficulty.

Translating the finding into classrooms raises its own complications. Frequent quizzes can provoke anxiety if they carry high stakes, and students left without feedback may repeatedly retrieve mistaken answers. Consequently, most researchers recommend low-stakes quizzes accompanied by corrective feedback rather than simply more examinations.

ra-ts056.t: When Do Children Understand False Beliefs?
ra-ts056.x:
A central milestone in cognitive development is the recognition that other people can hold beliefs that differ from reality. Researchers have traditionally assessed this ability with false-belief tasks. In a common version, a child watches a puppet place a toy in a basket and leave; while the puppet is away, the toy is moved to a box. Asked where the puppet will look for the toy on returning, most three-year-olds point to the box, where the toy actually is, whereas most children of four or five correctly choose the basket.

This finding was long taken to show that an understanding of false belief emerges around age four. Since the mid-2000s, however, studies measuring where infants look, rather than what they say, have challenged that conclusion. In some experiments, children not yet two years old looked longer when a character searched in a location that conflicted with the character's false belief, as if surprised.

How to reconcile these results is disputed. Some researchers argue that infants possess a genuine but implicit grasp of belief that verbal tasks, with their heavy demands on language and self-control, fail to reveal. Others suspect that the infant findings reflect simpler processes, such as tracking where an agent last saw an object, and note that several looking-time results have proved difficult to replicate.

ra-ts057.x:
Many Roman structures built with concrete, from harbor walls to the dome of the Pantheon, have survived for roughly two thousand years, whereas modern concrete exposed to the elements often begins to deteriorate within decades. Explaining this durability has occupied engineers and materials scientists for more than a century, and several factors appear to be involved.

One factor is the ingredients. Roman builders mixed lime with volcanic ash, notably from the area around the Bay of Naples, producing a binder that reacts chemically over long periods. In marine structures, analyses suggest that seawater percolating through the concrete gradually encouraged the growth of interlocking mineral crystals, including a rare form called aluminous tobermorite, which may have reinforced the material rather than weakening it. More recently, researchers have proposed that small white lumps of lime, once dismissed as evidence of careless mixing, could have acted as reservoirs of calcium, allowing cracks to seal themselves when water seeped in.

Such findings should not be overstated. The structures that survive are, by definition, the successful ones; countless poorly made Roman buildings have vanished. Roman concrete was also weaker in compression than many modern mixes and was rarely reinforced with steel, so it could not simply replace today's materials. Its value may lie instead in suggesting additives for more durable, lower-carbon concretes.

ra-ts058.x:
The universe is expanding, and the rate of that expansion today is expressed as the Hubble constant. For decades astronomers hoped that improved measurements would converge on a single value. Instead, two broad families of methods now yield results that disagree by roughly eight percent, a discrepancy known as the Hubble tension.

The first approach works outward from nearby objects. Astronomers measure the distances to pulsating stars called Cepheid variables, use these stars to calibrate the brightness of certain supernovae in more distant galaxies, and compare the resulting distances with how fast the galaxies are receding. The second approach works from the early universe: measurements of the cosmic microwave background, radiation released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, are combined with the standard cosmological model to predict the expansion rate today. The local method consistently gives the higher figure.

As the precision of both methods has improved, the gap has persisted rather than closing, which makes simple measurement error a less comfortable explanation. Some astronomers continue to suspect subtle problems in the distance ladder, such as the effects of dust or crowded star fields on Cepheid observations, and independent techniques based on other kinds of stars have given mixed results. Others regard the tension as a possible sign that the standard model is incomplete, perhaps missing some form of energy that acted in the early universe.

ra-ts059.t: What Ended the Age of Dinosaurs?
ra-ts059.x:
About 66 million years ago, roughly three-quarters of plant and animal species disappeared, among them all non-avian dinosaurs. In 1980 a team led by the physicist Luis Alvarez and his son, the geologist Walter Alvarez, reported unusually high concentrations of iridium, an element rare in Earth's crust but common in many meteorites, in a thin clay layer marking this boundary. They proposed that a large asteroid had struck the planet. The later identification of the Chicxulub crater, buried beneath the Yucatán Peninsula and some 180 kilometers across, persuaded most researchers that an impact had occurred at about the right time.

A rival explanation points to the Deccan Traps of western India, an enormous sequence of lava flows erupted over hundreds of thousands of years around the same interval. Such eruptions would have released vast quantities of carbon dioxide and sulfur gases, potentially disrupting climate long before and after the boundary.

Increasingly precise dating has turned an either-or debate into a question of proportion. Most specialists consider the impact the decisive blow, given the abruptness of the extinction in many fossil records. Some argue, however, that volcanism had already stressed ecosystems, leaving them more vulnerable; others maintain that its effects were too gradual to matter much. The relative contributions remain under active study.

ra-ts060.t: Why Did Industrialization Begin in Britain?
ra-ts060.x:
Historians broadly agree that mechanized industry first took hold in Britain in the late eighteenth century, beginning with cotton spinning and the steam engine. Why it began there, rather than in other commercially advanced regions such as the Netherlands, northern Italy or the Yangtze Delta, is far less settled.

One influential explanation emphasizes relative prices. According to this view, wages in Britain were unusually high compared with those elsewhere, while coal, abundant and close to the surface, was unusually cheap. Machines that substituted cheap energy and capital for expensive labor were therefore more profitable to adopt in Britain than in places where labor was cheap, which would account for why inventions such as the spinning jenny were developed and used there first. Critics of this account question the wage data on which it rests and point out that high wages alone do not generate new ideas.

A second family of explanations stresses culture and institutions: secure property rights, a growing community of skilled mechanics, and a culture that valued practical, experimental knowledge. Proponents argue that these conditions encouraged people to invent and share improvements. Many historians now suspect the answer lies in some combination of the two, with economic incentives determining which ideas were worth pursuing and a favorable intellectual climate supplying the ideas themselves.

ra-ps001.x:
Comets are small bodies made of ice, dust and rock. Scientists sometimes call them 'dirty snowballs'. Most of the time, a comet travels far away from the Sun, where it is very cold. Out there, a comet is just a frozen object a few kilometers wide, and it has no tail at all.

Things change when a comet's orbit brings it closer to the Sun. The Sun's heat turns some of the ice directly into gas. This gas, together with dust, forms a large, glowing cloud around the solid center of the comet. This cloud is called the coma, and it can be much bigger than the Earth.

Many comets then form two tails. One tail is made of dust. It is often curved, and it reflects sunlight, so it looks white or yellow. The other tail is made of gas. Energy from the Sun makes this gas glow with a bluish color, and the solar wind, a stream of tiny particles from the Sun, pushes it into a straight line. Both tails point away from the Sun, not behind the comet. Because of this, a comet that is moving away from the Sun actually travels tail first.

ra-ps002.x:
A plant cannot walk, but its seeds can travel a long way. Moving away from the parent plant is important for a seed. If it falls right under its parent, the young plant must compete with the parent for light, water and space. Plants have developed several ways to send their seeds to new places.

Some plants use the wind. A dandelion seed has a tiny 'parachute' of soft hairs, and a maple seed has a flat wing that makes it spin as it falls. These shapes keep the seeds in the air longer, so the wind can carry them farther.

Other plants use animals. Many fruits, such as berries, are sweet and brightly colored. Birds and other animals eat them, and the seeds pass through the animal's body and are dropped somewhere else. Some seeds, such as burdock, have small hooks that stick to fur or clothing. In fact, these hooks gave an engineer the idea for the hook-and-loop fastener used on shoes and bags. Water can move seeds too. A coconut can float in the sea for weeks and then grow on a beach far from its home. Finally, a few plants, like some peas, simply shoot their seeds out when their pods dry and burst open.

ra-ps003.t: Music in the Age of Silent Film
ra-ps003.x:
Films made before the late 1920s are called 'silent films' because they had no recorded sound. However, audiences at the time rarely watched them in silence. In most theaters, live music played during every show. In small theaters, a single pianist often played. Larger theaters might have an organ or even a full orchestra. The musicians watched the screen and changed the music to match the action. Fast music went with chase scenes, and slow, soft music went with sad or romantic moments. Music also covered the noise of the projector and the audience.

At first, many players made up the music as they went along. Later, film companies began to send cue sheets with their films. A cue sheet was a list that suggested which pieces of music to play during each scene. For some important films, composers wrote complete scores, so the music was planned as carefully as the pictures.

When films with recorded sound arrived, thousands of theater musicians lost their jobs within a few years. Today, however, some cinemas and festivals show old silent films with live music again, so modern audiences can enjoy them the way people did about a hundred years ago.

ra-ps004.x:
In the early 1800s, moving goods across the United States was slow and expensive. Roads were rough, and wagons pulled by horses could carry only small loads. Farmers in the west had trouble selling their crops in the big cities on the east coast.

To solve this problem, the state of New York built the Erie Canal. Work began in 1817, and the canal opened in 1825. It ran about 363 miles (584 kilometers) from Albany, on the Hudson River, to Buffalo, on Lake Erie. Thousands of workers dug it mostly by hand, using shovels, horses and simple machines. Because the land rose and fell along the way, the builders added dozens of locks. A lock is a section of canal with gates at each end that raises or lowers boats from one water level to another.

The canal was a great success. Boats pulled by mules walking on a path beside the water could carry far more than wagons. The cost of shipping goods dropped sharply, and trips became much faster. Towns along the route grew quickly, and New York City became the most important port in the country. Later, railroads took much of the canal's business, but parts of it are still used today, mostly by pleasure boats.

ra-ps005.t: Ice, Albedo, and a Warming Arctic
ra-ps005.x:
Different surfaces on Earth reflect different amounts of sunlight, a property scientists call albedo. Fresh snow and sea ice have a high albedo, reflecting most of the sunlight that reaches them, while open ocean water has a low albedo and absorbs most of it. This difference plays an important role in the climate of the polar regions.

When the Arctic warms, some sea ice melts, exposing darker water beneath. The water absorbs more solar energy than the ice did, which warms the ocean and causes still more ice to melt. Because the initial warming leads to changes that produce further warming, this process is known as a positive feedback. It is one reason the Arctic has warmed considerably faster than the global average in recent decades.

Satellite measurements since the late 1970s show that the area covered by Arctic sea ice at the end of summer has declined markedly, although the amount varies from year to year with weather patterns. Researchers point out that the feedback also works in reverse: in cold periods, expanding ice reflects more sunlight and reinforces cooling. Other factors, including changes in clouds and ocean currents, also influence Arctic temperatures, so albedo is an important part of the story but not the whole of it.

ra-ps006.x:
Teachers often say that they truly understood a subject only after they had to explain it to others. Education researchers have tested this idea, sometimes called the protégé effect, and much of the evidence supports it. Students who tutor younger classmates, for example, frequently improve their own understanding of the material, not only the understanding of the students they help.

Interestingly, some of the benefit seems to appear even before any teaching takes place. In several experiments, participants who were told they would later have to teach a passage to someone else remembered it better and organized it more clearly than participants who were told they would simply be tested. Researchers suggest that expecting to teach changes how people study: they look for the main ideas, notice how the ideas connect, and anticipate questions a learner might ask.

Actually explaining the material may add further benefits. To explain something, a person must put it into their own words, and gaps in understanding quickly become obvious. However, the effect is not automatic. Tutors who simply read their notes aloud gain little, and the benefit appears to depend on whether they have to answer questions and produce explanations themselves. For this reason, many teachers now ask students to explain ideas to a partner during class.

ra-ps007.x:
Adults know that an object continues to exist even when it cannot be seen. A ball that rolls under a sofa is still there. This understanding, called object permanence, is not something infants appear to have from birth, or at least not in an obvious form.

The Swiss psychologist Jean Piaget studied this ability in the mid-twentieth century. He noticed that if a young infant watched a toy being covered with a cloth, the infant usually did not try to search for it, as if the toy had stopped existing. According to Piaget, infants begin to search for hidden objects at around eight or nine months, and their understanding continues to develop into the second year of life.

Later researchers questioned whether Piaget's tests measured what infants knew or simply what they could do. Searching requires planning and controlled movement of the hands, which young infants have not yet mastered. In the 1980s, researchers began measuring how long infants looked at events instead, because babies tend to stare longer at things that surprise them. In some studies, infants only a few months old looked longer when an object seemed to pass through a hidden barrier, suggesting they expected the object to still exist. However, some psychologists argue that longer looking does not necessarily show true understanding.

ra-ps008.x:
Most fossils are the remains of an organism's body, such as bones, teeth or shells. Trace fossils are different: they record the activity of living animals. Footprints, burrows, nests and even bite marks can all be preserved. Of these, fossil footprints, or trackways, are among the most informative.

A single footprint can suggest what kind of animal made it, but a series of prints reveals behavior that bones cannot. By measuring the length of a stride and comparing it with the size of the foot, paleontologists can estimate how fast an animal was moving. Most dinosaur trackways show animals walking at a moderate pace, though a few suggest running. When many parallel trackways of the same species are found together, they may indicate that the animals traveled in groups.

Trace fossils have limitations, however. It is often difficult to match a footprint to a particular species, because bones are rarely found at the end of a trail. Footprints can also be distorted by the softness of the mud in which they were made, so the same animal might leave quite different prints on different ground. For these reasons, paleontologists usually treat conclusions from trackways as strong suggestions rather than certainties.

ra-ps009.x:
A traditional picture of science treats observation as a neutral foundation: researchers first gather facts, and only afterward construct theories to explain them. In the mid-twentieth century, philosophers such as Norwood Russell Hanson challenged this picture by arguing that observation is 'theory-laden'. What a scientist sees, on this view, is shaped by the concepts and expectations he or she already holds. Hanson illustrated the point by asking whether two astronomers with different theories, watching the same sunrise, would really see the same thing.

The thesis has a moderate and a radical form. The moderate version holds merely that trained observers notice and describe things that novices miss; a radiologist reading an X-ray perceives a fracture where a layperson sees only shadows. Few dispute this. The radical version claims that scientists committed to rival theories inhabit, in a sense, different perceptual worlds, so that observation cannot settle disputes between them.

Critics have objected that the radical version proves too much. If observation were wholly determined by theory, it is hard to see how experiments could ever surprise researchers, yet unexpected results occur regularly and sometimes overturn cherished assumptions. Many philosophers therefore adopt an intermediate position: observation is never entirely free of interpretation, but it is constrained enough by the world to serve as a shared, if fallible, check on competing theories.

ra-ps010.x:
In the 1970s, measurements by astronomers including Vera Rubin showed that stars in the outer regions of spiral galaxies orbit far faster than expected. If the only mass present were the visible stars and gas, those outer stars should move more slowly, much as distant planets in our solar system orbit the Sun more slowly than nearby ones. The most widely accepted explanation is that galaxies are embedded in vast halos of dark matter, an invisible substance that exerts gravity but neither emits nor absorbs light.

A minority of physicists favor a different interpretation. In 1983 Mordehai Milgrom proposed Modified Newtonian Dynamics, or MOND, which holds that gravity itself behaves differently at extremely low accelerations, such as those experienced by stars at the edges of galaxies. MOND predicts the rotation of many individual galaxies with striking accuracy and without any invisible matter.

The difficulty for MOND lies at larger scales. Observations of galaxy clusters, of the way massive objects bend light from more distant sources, and of the cosmic microwave background are, most cosmologists argue, far more naturally explained by dark matter. Yet decades of experiments designed to detect dark matter particles directly have so far found none. Each side, in other words, can point to phenomena the other explains less comfortably, which is why the debate has not been settled.

ra-ps011.t: The Gold Standard Between the Wars
ra-ps011.x:
Before 1914, many leading economies tied their currencies to gold, promising to exchange notes for a fixed quantity of the metal. The arrangement was widely credited with promoting stable exchange rates and international trade. Suspended in 1914, it was gradually restored in the 1920s, most famously when Britain returned to gold in 1925 at its prewar rate, a decision that many economists, including John Maynard Keynes, criticized for overvaluing the pound.

Since the 1980s, a number of economic historians have argued that the restored system helped turn a downturn into the Great Depression. Under gold-standard rules, a country losing gold reserves had to raise interest rates and restrict the money supply, even when its economy was already contracting. Because currencies were linked, these deflationary pressures spread from one country to another.

The strongest evidence for this view is comparative: countries that left gold earlier, such as Britain in 1931, generally began to recover sooner than those that held on longer, such as France. Some scholars caution, however, that the timing of departure was not random. Countries may have abandoned gold partly because their circumstances differed, which complicates any simple inference about cause and effect. Nevertheless, the association is consistent enough that most economists now regard adherence to gold as a significant contributor to the depth of the slump.

ra-ps012.t: The Many Origins of C4 Photosynthesis
ra-ps012.x:
Most plants capture carbon dioxide using an enzyme called Rubisco, which has a notable weakness: it sometimes reacts with oxygen instead, wasting energy in a process known as photorespiration. The problem worsens at high temperatures and when carbon dioxide is scarce. Some plants, including maize, sugarcane and many tropical grasses, have evolved a solution called C4 photosynthesis. They first fix carbon in outer leaf cells and then deliver it in concentrated form to inner cells where Rubisco operates, so that the enzyme encounters far less oxygen.

What makes C4 photosynthesis remarkable is not only its efficiency but its history. Rather than arising once and spreading, it appears to have evolved independently more than sixty times in different plant lineages, an exceptional case of convergent evolution for a trait involving so many coordinated changes in anatomy and biochemistry.

Why it emerged so often, and mostly within the past thirty million years, is debated. One prominent hypothesis links its rise to a long-term decline in atmospheric carbon dioxide, which would have made photorespiration more costly. Others emphasize hot, dry or open habitats, noting that the major expansion of C4 grasslands seems to have occurred millions of years after carbon dioxide had already fallen. Many botanists suspect that falling carbon dioxide made C4 advantageous in principle, while climate and ecology determined where and when it actually spread.

ra-ts001.x:
The Namib Desert along the southwestern coast of Africa receives almost no rain, yet several species of darkling beetle survive there by drinking water they collect from the air. On many mornings, fog rolls in from the cold Atlantic Ocean, carrying tiny droplets that are far too small to fall as rain. The beetles have developed a remarkable way to capture this moisture before the sun burns the fog away.

In a behavior known as fog basking, a beetle climbs to the top of a sand dune, faces the wind, and tilts its body forward so that its back points toward the incoming fog. The surface of its hard wing covers is not uniform. Small bumps attract water, while the areas between them have a waxy coating that repels it. Droplets cling to the bumps and grow until they become heavy enough to roll down the beetle's back toward its mouth.

Engineers have studied this design closely because it suggests a low-cost way to gather water in dry regions. Experimental fog nets and surface coatings inspired by the beetle combine water-attracting and water-repelling materials, in an attempt to improve on the simple mesh nets already used in some coastal villages.

ra-ts002.t: Glacial Erratics: Boulders Out of Place
ra-ts002.x:
Across parts of North America and northern Europe, travelers sometimes find a huge boulder sitting alone in a field or forest, made of a type of rock completely different from the bedrock beneath it. Geologists call such stones glacial erratics. For centuries, their presence puzzled observers, and some early explanations suggested that the boulders had been carried by enormous floods.

In the nineteenth century, scientists including the Swiss-born naturalist Louis Agassiz argued that the stones had been moved by ice. During the ice ages, vast glaciers spread across these regions. As the ice advanced, it plucked loose rock from the land and carried it along, sometimes for hundreds of kilometers. When the climate warmed and the glaciers melted, the rocks were simply dropped where the ice had left them.

Today erratics are valuable evidence. By matching the mineral makeup of a boulder to the bedrock at its source, researchers can trace the path that a glacier followed. In this way, a single out-of-place rock can reveal the direction of ice movement thousands of years ago.

ra-ts003.t: Why We Always See the Same Side of the Moon
ra-ts003.x:
Anyone who watches the Moon over many months notices that its familiar pattern of dark and light areas never changes. This happens because the Moon takes the same time to spin once on its axis as it does to orbit Earth, about 27 days. Astronomers describe this condition as tidal locking.

The cause is gravity. Earth's pull stretches the Moon slightly, raising a small bulge on the side facing Earth and another on the far side. Early in its history, the Moon probably rotated faster, so these bulges were constantly being pulled out of line with Earth. Earth's gravity tugged on them, acting like a brake, and gradually slowed the Moon's spin until the bulges stayed pointed at Earth. Once that happened, the slowing stopped.

Tidal locking is common in the solar system. Many large moons of Jupiter and Saturn always show one face to their planets. The process also works in the other direction: the Moon's gravity is slowly lengthening Earth's day, although the change amounts to only a tiny fraction of a second each century.

ra-ts004.x:
Trees in temperate climates add one growth ring each year. In a good year, with plenty of rain and mild temperatures, the ring is wide; in a dry or cold year, it is narrow. Because weather affects trees of a species across a region in a similar way, trees growing in the same area share the same sequence of wide and narrow rings. This fact is the basis of dendrochronology, the science of dating wood by its rings.

Researchers begin with living trees, whose outermost ring is known to belong to the current year. They then match the inner rings of these trees with the outer rings of older dead trees or timber from old buildings. By overlapping many samples, they build a continuous record that stretches back far beyond the life of any single tree. In some regions, such records now cover more than ten thousand years.

For archaeologists, this record is extremely useful. A wooden beam from an ancient house can be compared with the master sequence to find the year the tree was cut down. Unlike many other dating methods, which give a range of possible dates, tree rings can sometimes provide a precise calendar year.

ra-ts005.x:
Painters in medieval Europe often showed important figures larger than less important ones, and they paid little attention to whether buildings and floors looked realistic. In the early fifteenth century, however, artists in Florence began to use a mathematical system for creating the illusion of depth on a flat surface. This system is known as linear perspective.

The architect Filippo Brunelleschi is usually credited with demonstrating the method. He painted a view of a famous building in Florence and showed that, when seen through a small hole and reflected in a mirror, the painting matched the real scene almost exactly. A few years later, the writer Leon Battista Alberti described the rules in a book for painters. According to these rules, lines that are parallel in reality, such as the edges of a road, should be drawn so that they meet at a single vanishing point on the horizon. Objects become smaller at a regular rate as they move toward that point.

The new technique spread quickly. Within decades, painters across Italy were building their compositions around carefully measured grids, and viewers came to expect pictures to look like windows onto real space.

ra-ts006.x:
When people try to remember a list of words, they do not recall every item equally well. In typical experiments, participants hear a list of about fifteen to twenty words and then write down as many as they can, in any order. The results form a U-shaped pattern: words at the beginning and end of the list are remembered much better than those in the middle. Psychologists call this the serial position effect.

The advantage for early items is known as the primacy effect. One explanation is that people have more time to repeat the first few words to themselves before new ones arrive, which helps move them into long-term memory. The advantage for the last items, called the recency effect, seems to have a different cause. These words are still held in short-term memory when the person starts writing.

Evidence for this distinction comes from studies that add a short delay before recall. If participants must count backward for about thirty seconds after hearing the list, the recency effect largely disappears, while the primacy effect remains. The counting task pushes the last words out of short-term memory but does not erase words that have already been stored.

ra-ts007.x:
In the sixteenth century, the English financier Sir Thomas Gresham advised the queen about the poor state of the country's coins. The principle he described, later named Gresham's law, is often summarized in a short phrase: bad money drives out good. Though Gresham was not the first to notice it, his name became attached to the idea.

The law applies when two forms of money are legally required to have the same value but are worth different amounts as material. In the past, coins were made of silver or gold, and some had been clipped at the edges or mixed with cheaper metal. If a full-weight coin and a damaged one could both pay for the same loaf of bread, people naturally spent the damaged coins and kept the good ones at home, melted them down, or sent them abroad. Before long, only the poorer coins remained in circulation.

Economists note that the law depends on fixed official values. When people are free to refuse poor coins or to accept them only at a discount, good money can stay in use, and the effect may even reverse.

ra-ts008.x:
English spelling often seems strange to learners. Why, for example, is the letter 'i' in 'time' pronounced so differently from the 'i' in many other European languages? Much of the answer lies in a series of sound changes known as the Great Vowel Shift, which took place in England roughly between 1400 and 1700.

During this period, the long vowels of English gradually moved to new positions in the mouth. Most were raised, meaning they came to be pronounced with the tongue higher. The word 'meet', for instance, once had a vowel closer to the one now heard in 'mate'. The two highest long vowels could not rise any further, so they became diphthongs, or combinations of two vowel sounds. That is why 'time', once pronounced somewhat like 'teem', now contains a sound that glides from one vowel to another.

Spelling, meanwhile, was becoming fixed. The printing press, introduced to England in the 1470s, encouraged standard spellings that were based largely on older pronunciations. As a result, many English words are still written the way they were said before the shift was complete.

ra-ts009.x:
Long before the electrical telegraph, France built a national network that could send messages hundreds of kilometers in a matter of hours or even minutes. Its designer, the inventor Claude Chappe, tested the system in the early 1790s, and the first line, linking Paris with the northern city of Lille, began operating in 1794.

The system relied on a chain of towers placed on hills, usually ten to fifteen kilometers apart. On top of each tower stood a wooden beam with two smaller movable arms at its ends. Operators turned handles to set the beam and arms into different positions, each of which stood for a letter, a number, or a whole word or phrase listed in a codebook. An operator in the next tower watched through a telescope, copied the signal, and passed it on.

The network eventually grew to more than five hundred stations. It had obvious limits, however. Fog, rain, and darkness could stop transmission completely, and the system required large numbers of trained staff. When electrical telegraph lines, which worked in any weather, spread in the mid-nineteenth century, the towers were gradually abandoned.

ra-ts010.t: Fungi and the Roots of Trees
ra-ts010.x:
Most land plants live in partnership with fungi. Fine fungal threads, called hyphae, wrap around or grow into a plant's roots and spread far into the surrounding soil. This association, known as mycorrhiza, is ancient; fossil evidence suggests that fungi helped some of the earliest plants colonize land more than 400 million years ago.

The arrangement benefits both partners. Because hyphae are much thinner than roots, they can reach into tiny spaces between soil particles and absorb water and nutrients such as phosphorus that roots alone would miss. The fungi pass some of these resources to the plant. In return, the plant supplies the fungi with sugars it produces through photosynthesis, which the fungi cannot make for themselves.

In forests, a single fungus may connect the roots of several trees at once, forming what some researchers call a common mycorrhizal network. Experiments using traceable forms of carbon have shown that materials can move between trees through such links. How much this exchange matters for the trees' survival in natural forests, however, is still debated among scientists.

ra-ts011.t: The Rise and Fall of Sunspots
ra-ts011.x:
Seen through a properly filtered telescope, the surface of the Sun is often marked by dark patches called sunspots. They appear dark only by comparison: a sunspot is more than a thousand degrees Celsius cooler than the surrounding surface, yet it would still shine brightly if it could be seen on its own. Sunspots form where strong magnetic fields break through the surface and block some of the heat rising from below.

The number of sunspots is not constant. In the nineteenth century, the German amateur astronomer Heinrich Schwabe observed the Sun almost daily for years while searching for an unknown planet close to the Sun. He never found the planet, but he noticed that sunspots rise and fall in number over a period of about eleven years. At solar minimum, weeks may pass without a single spot; at solar maximum, dozens can be visible at once.

The cycle matters beyond astronomy. Periods of high sunspot activity also bring more solar flares and eruptions of charged particles. When these particles reach Earth, they can produce bright auroras, but they can also disturb radio communication, satellites, and power grids. For this reason, space agencies now monitor the Sun continuously.

ra-ts012.t: Ancient Pollen as a Record of the Past
ra-ts012.x:
Every spring and summer, plants release enormous quantities of pollen into the air. Most grains never reach another flower. Instead, many settle on the surfaces of lakes and bogs, sink to the bottom, and are buried in layers of mud. Because the outer wall of a pollen grain is extremely tough, these grains can survive for thousands of years in places where oxygen is scarce.

Scientists who study ancient pollen, known as palynologists, drill long cores of sediment from such sites. Each layer represents a period of time, with the oldest at the bottom. Under a microscope, pollen from different plants can usually be identified by its size, shape, and surface pattern. By counting the grains of each type in each layer, researchers can reconstruct how the surrounding vegetation changed over time.

This method has become an important tool in archaeology. A sudden fall in tree pollen together with a rise in pollen from grasses and cereal crops, for example, often marks the moment when early farmers cleared forests to plant fields. In this way, pollen can reveal human activity even at sites where few objects have been found.

ra-ts013.x:
In 1854, Japan, which had limited its contact with the outside world for more than two centuries, agreed to open several ports to foreign ships. Within a few years, Japanese goods were arriving in Europe in large numbers, and among them were colorful woodblock prints known as ukiyo-e. These prints, produced cheaply in great quantities for ordinary buyers in Japan, quickly attracted the attention of artists in Paris.

The prints looked very different from European painting. Instead of creating deep space through linear perspective and shading, artists such as Hokusai and Hiroshige used flat areas of bright color, strong outlines, and unusual viewpoints. Their compositions were often asymmetrical, with figures or objects cut off sharply by the edge of the picture. Ordinary moments, such as people crossing a bridge in the rain, were treated as worthy subjects.

Many painters linked with Impressionism and the movements that followed collected these prints and borrowed their ideas. Edgar Degas cropped his figures at the edges of his canvases, while Vincent van Gogh made careful painted copies of prints by Hiroshige.
