The French fashion for Japanese art became so widespread that critics gave it a name: Japonisme.

ra-ts014.x:
Students preparing for an exam often study in one long session the night before. Research on memory suggests that this is an inefficient strategy. When the same total amount of study time is divided into several shorter sessions spread over days or weeks, people usually remember the material far longer. This finding, called the spacing effect, was first described in the 1880s by the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus, who tested his own memory for lists of meaningless syllables.

Since then, the effect has been confirmed in hundreds of studies with learners of all ages and with many kinds of material, from vocabulary to mathematics. Psychologists have proposed several explanations. One is that a gap between sessions allows some forgetting to occur, so the learner must work harder to recall the information at the next session, and this effort makes the memory stronger.

Despite this evidence, spacing is less popular than cramming. One reason is that cramming feels effective: immediately after a long session, the material seems familiar, and learners mistake this familiarity for lasting knowledge. A test a week later usually shows the difference clearly.

ra-ts015.x:
When people who share no common language need to communicate regularly, for trade or work, they sometimes develop a simplified form of speech called a pidgin. A pidgin usually takes most of its vocabulary from one dominant language but has a small number of words and very simple grammar. It is no one's first language; speakers use it only for limited purposes and return to their own languages at home.

Something remarkable can happen in the next generation. If children grow up hearing a pidgin as their main language, they expand it into a full language with a large vocabulary and consistent grammar. Such a language is called a creole. Creoles can express anything that other languages can, and they are learned and spoken as native languages by entire communities.

Tok Pisin, spoken in Papua New Guinea, is a well-known example. It began as a pidgin based mostly on English vocabulary, but it has become the first language of many families and is used by millions of people. Today it is one of the country's official languages and appears in newspapers, on the radio, and in parliament.

ra-ts016.t: Harrison's Sea Clock and the Longitude Problem
ra-ts016.x:
For centuries, sailors on long ocean voyages could find their latitude, their position north or south, by measuring the height of the Sun or certain stars. Longitude, their position east or west, was far harder to determine. Because Earth turns 15 degrees every hour, a navigator who knew the exact time at a home port could compare it with local time at sea and calculate how far east or west the ship had traveled. The problem was keeping accurate time aboard a moving ship.

Pendulum clocks, the most accurate timekeepers of the period, were useless at sea, where the rolling of the ship disturbed their swing and changes in temperature and humidity affected their parts. In 1714, the British government offered a large prize for a practical solution. John Harrison, a carpenter and self-taught clockmaker, spent decades building a series of sea clocks. His fourth design, which resembled a large pocket watch, kept remarkably accurate time during a voyage to the Caribbean in 1761 and 1762.

Although Harrison struggled for years to receive full payment, his work proved that the time method could succeed. Within decades, marine chronometers became standard equipment on ocean-going ships.

ra-ts017.x:
In simple economic models, prices adjust immediately whenever supply or demand changes. In the real world, however, many prices stay the same for months, even when a business's costs have risen or fallen. Economists use the term 'sticky prices' for this behavior, and one of the best-known explanations for it involves what are called menu costs.

The name comes from restaurants. Changing prices means printing new menus, and that costs money and time. More generally, menu costs include any expense connected with changing a price: relabeling goods on shelves, updating catalogs and price lists, reprogramming cash registers, and informing customers. If a firm expects only a small gain from adjusting a price, these costs may make it sensible to leave the price unchanged for a while.

Menu costs help explain why prices often change in occasional large steps rather than continuously. They also have consequences for the whole economy, since slow price adjustment can affect how quickly an economy responds to changes in spending. Some economists argue that digital price tags and online shopping, which make price changes almost free, may gradually reduce the importance of this explanation.

ra-ts018.t: Pine Cones That Wait for Fire
ra-ts018.x:
In many forests, fire is not only a destructive force but also a normal part of the ecosystem. Some trees have adapted so closely to periodic fires that they depend on them to reproduce. The lodgepole pine of western North America is a well-known example.

Many lodgepole pines produce cones that are sealed shut with a thick resin. These cones, described as serotinous, can remain closed on the branches for years, holding seeds that are still alive. Ordinary summer warmth is not enough to open them. When a fire passes through the forest, however, the intense heat melts the resin, and the cone scales slowly open. In the days after the fire, the seeds fall onto the ground.

The timing gives the seedlings important advantages. The fire has cleared away the plants that would otherwise compete with them for light and water, and the ash adds nutrients to the soil. As a result, a burned lodgepole forest often fills with thousands of young pines within a few years. Ecologists note, though, that this strategy works best when fires are spaced far enough apart for new trees to mature and produce cones of their own.

ra-ts019.x:
Chameleons are famous for changing color, and many people believe they do so mainly to match their surroundings. In fact, research suggests that color change in many species is used more for communication and for controlling body temperature than for hiding. A male may become brighter to attract a female or to warn a rival, and a darker skin can absorb more heat on a cool morning.

For a long time, scientists assumed that chameleons changed color only by spreading or concentrating grains of pigment in their skin cells, as many other animals do. Studies of panther chameleons published in the 2010s pointed to an additional mechanism. Beneath the outer pigment layer lies a layer of cells containing tiny crystals arranged in a regular pattern. By adjusting this layer, the animal changes the distance between the crystals, which in turn changes which colors of light are reflected. When the crystals are close together, the skin reflects mainly blue light; when they move apart, longer wavelengths such as yellow and red are reflected.

This kind of color, produced by structure rather than by pigment, is also seen in butterfly wings and bird feathers.

ra-ts020.x:
Some of the world's largest cave systems form in limestone, a rock made mostly of the mineral calcite. Limestone dissolves only very slowly in pure water, but rainwater is rarely pure. As it falls through the air and soaks through soil, it picks up carbon dioxide and becomes a weak acid. When this slightly acidic water seeps into cracks in limestone, it gradually dissolves the rock and carries the calcite away.

Over hundreds of thousands of years, small cracks widen into passages and chambers. Landscapes shaped in this way are called karst. On the surface, they are often marked by sinkholes, where the ground has collapsed into empty spaces below, and by streams that suddenly disappear underground.

Inside the caves, the same chemistry can work in reverse. When water carrying dissolved calcite drips from a cave ceiling, it releases some of its carbon dioxide into the cave air. The water can then no longer hold all of its calcite, and a tiny ring of mineral is left behind. Drop by drop, these deposits build stalactites hanging from the ceiling, while water landing on the floor builds stalagmites that grow upward to meet them.

ra-ts021.x:
Most volcanoes form near the edges of tectonic plates, the huge slabs of rock that make up Earth's outer shell. The Hawaiian Islands are an exception. They lie in the middle of the Pacific Plate, thousands of kilometers from the nearest plate boundary. To explain them, the Canadian geophysicist J. Tuzo Wilson proposed in 1963 that a fixed hot spot deep beneath the plate supplies magma to the surface.

According to this idea, the Pacific Plate moves slowly northwest over the hot spot, at a rate of several centimeters per year. Magma rising from below builds a volcano on the sea floor, which may grow tall enough to become an island. As the plate carries the volcano away, it is cut off from its supply of magma and becomes extinct, and a new volcano begins to form over the hot spot.

The theory explains a striking pattern. The island of Hawaii, at the southeastern end of the chain, has active volcanoes, while the islands become steadily older toward the northwest. The oldest islands have been worn down by erosion and have sunk, and beyond them lies a long line of underwater mountains.

ra-ts022.x:
Many structures built by the ancient Romans are still standing after two thousand years, including harbor walls that have been exposed to seawater for centuries. Modern concrete, by contrast, can begin to crack and crumble within decades, especially in the sea. This difference has led researchers to look closely at what the Romans put into their building material.

Roman concrete was made by mixing lime with volcanic ash and chunks of rock. The ash, found in large amounts near the Bay of Naples, reacted with the lime to form a strong binding material. In marine structures, the Romans packed this mixture into wooden forms placed in the sea. Studies of samples taken from ancient harbors suggest that seawater slowly reacting with the ash produced new minerals inside the concrete. These minerals grew in the spaces and cracks, which may have made the material stronger over time instead of weaker.

Roman concrete had disadvantages, too. It gained strength slowly and could not support the heavy loads that modern reinforced concrete carries. Even so, engineers are studying its chemistry for ideas that could make modern concrete longer-lasting.

ra-ts023.t: The Bullhorn Acacia and Its Ants
ra-ts023.x:
In Central America, the bullhorn acacia and certain species of ants have one of the best-studied partnerships in nature. The tree is named for its large, hollow thorns, which look like the horns of a bull. Ant colonies live inside these thorns, chewing an entrance hole near the tip and raising their young within.

The tree also feeds its guests. Glands at the base of its leaves produce a sugary nectar, and the tips of young leaflets bear small, protein-rich structures known as Beltian bodies, named after the naturalist Thomas Belt, who described them in the nineteenth century. The ants harvest these structures and feed them to their larvae.

In return, the ants defend the tree aggressively. They sting and bite insects and even large mammals that try to eat the leaves, and they cut back vines and seedlings of other plants growing close to their host. Experiments in which ants were removed from young acacias showed the value of this protection: without their defenders, the trees were damaged much more heavily by plant-eating insects, and many grew slowly or died. The bullhorn acacia also lacks much of the chemical defense found in related species, apparently because the ants make it unnecessary.

ra-ts024.t: How Young Songbirds Learn to Sing
ra-ts024.x:
Many songbirds, including zebra finches and white-crowned sparrows, are not born knowing their songs. A young male must learn by listening to adult birds, usually his father or other males nearby. Researchers have studied this process for decades because it resembles, in some ways, the way human children learn to speak.

Learning happens in stages. First, during a period early in life, the young bird listens and forms a memory of the song it hears. Later, it begins to practice, producing quiet, rambling sounds that some scientists compare to the babbling of human infants. Over weeks of practice, the bird gradually adjusts its output until it matches the memorized model. Birds that are deafened before this practice stage cannot develop a normal song, which shows that they must hear themselves to compare their attempts with the memory.

Timing is also important. In several species, a bird that hears no adult song during its early sensitive period never develops a normal version, even if it hears the song later. Such birds produce simplified songs that lack many of the features of their species. In this respect, too, birdsong offers scientists a useful model for studying how the brain learns sounds.

Before first use

Fill the kettle with water to the MAX line and boil it once. Pour the water away. Do this two times to clean the inside.

Daily use

1. Open the lid and fill the kettle with fresh water. Never fill it above the MAX line or below the MIN line.
2. Close the lid until it clicks.
3. Place the kettle on its base and press the switch. The blue light turns on.
4. The kettle turns off by itself when the water boils. Wait a few seconds before you pour.

Care

If white marks appear inside the kettle, pour in a cup of white vinegar and a cup of water, boil it, and leave it for 20 minutes. Then rinse well. Always unplug the kettle before cleaning. Do not put the kettle or its base in water.

If the kettle does not work, check that the plug is in the wall and that the lid is closed properly.

rl-ps010.x:
Notice: Revised Procedure for Grade Appeals

Effective with the fall semester, the process by which students may contest a final course grade has been revised in order to ensure greater consistency across departments. Previously, a student who believed a grade to be unjust would approach the instructor informally and, if dissatisfied, write directly to the dean. Under the new procedure, a student must first submit a written request to the instructor within ten working days of the grades being posted, stating specifically which element of the assessment is disputed and why.

If the instructor does not reply within five working days or if the student remains unconvinced, the matter may be referred to a committee of three faculty members from outside the course. The committee's decision is final, save in cases where a procedural irregularity can be demonstrated. Students are encouraged to consult the Ombudsperson's office before filing, since it can offer confidential advice at no cost.

rl-ps011.x:
Global Scholars Fellowship: Call for Applications

The Global Scholars Fellowship supports early-career researchers whose work crosses national or disciplinary boundaries. Each year, up to eight fellows receive a stipend of $24,000 and funding of up to $6,000 for travel and materials. Fellowships run for ten months, during which fellows are expected to be in residence at a host institution abroad for at least six.

While publications are valued, the selection committee places particular weight on the clarity and originality of the research proposal, and on evidence that the applicant has thought critically about the choice of host institution. Proposals that merely extend a doctoral thesis without a distinct question are rarely successful. Candidates should have completed their doctorate within the past four years.

Applicants must submit a 1,500-word proposal, two letters of reference, and a letter of invitation from the host. Because invitations can take weeks to arrange, applicants are advised to approach prospective hosts early. Incomplete applications will not be considered, and no extensions are granted.

easy to find

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, how can paleontologists estimate how fast an animal was moving?
questions.e: Scientists measure 'the length of a stride' and compare it 'with the size of the foot'; a stride is the distance between steps. Counting parallel trackways tells them about group travel, not speed.
o: By counting how many trackways are found together
By comparing the distance between steps with the size of the foot
By measuring the bones found at the end of a trail
By testing how soft the mud was at the time when the prints were first made

questions.s: All of the following are given as limitations of trace fossils EXCEPT:
questions.e: The passage never says footprints are rare. The other options paraphrase paragraph 3: 'difficult to match a footprint to a particular species', 'bones are rarely found at the end of a trail', and prints 'distorted by the softness of the mud'.
o: Footprints are too rare to be studied.
It is hard to link a print to one species.
Bones are seldom found at the end of a trail.
Soft mud can change the shape of a print.

questions.s: Why does the author mention 'many parallel trackways of the same species'?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says trackways reveal 'behavior that bones cannot', and parallel trackways 'may indicate that the animals traveled in groups'. The first option is wrong because 'Most dinosaur trackways show animals walking at a moderate pace'.
o: To show that most dinosaurs ran very quickly
To give an example of behavior that footprints can reveal
To explain why some footprints become distorted
To show that the bones of the animals are often found close to their footprints

questions.s: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
questions.e: The passage presents the challenge to the 'neutral foundation' picture, two versions of the thesis, and an 'intermediate position'. The first option is the traditional view being challenged, and the third reverses the critics' rejection of the radical version.
o: Observation is a neutral foundation on which all scientific theories are built.
Trained radiologists see more in X-rays than people without medical training.
Most philosophers now accept the radical claim that rivals live in different perceptual worlds.
Philosophers debate how far theory shapes observation, and many take a middle view.

questions.s: Why does the author mention a radiologist reading an X-ray?
questions.e: The example follows 'The moderate version holds merely that trained observers notice ... things that novices miss'. It is not evidence for the radical version, which is introduced only afterward.
o: To show that medical images are often interpreted incorrectly
To support the claim that observation cannot settle disputes
To illustrate the moderate version of the thesis
To suggest that novices are more objective observers than experts

questions.s: The word 'fallible' in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: The phrase 'a shared, if fallible, check' means observation is a useful test even though it can sometimes be mistaken. 'Completely neutral' contradicts the same sentence, which says observation is 'never entirely free of interpretation'.
o: capable of being wrong
shared by everyone
easily changed
completely neutral

questions.s: The critics' point about unexpected results implies which of the following?
questions.e: The critics say that if observation 'were wholly determined by theory', it would be 'hard to see how experiments could ever surprise researchers'. The first and last options contradict the passage, which says surprises 'occur regularly'.
o: Experiments rarely produce outcomes that researchers did not predict.
If theory fully fixed what scientists saw, they would see only what they expected.
Unexpected results provide strong support for the radical version of the theory-laden thesis.
Cherished assumptions in science are almost never overturned by experiments.

questions.s: How is the passage organized?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 presents Hanson's challenge, paragraph 2 separates 'a moderate and a radical form', and paragraph 3 describes the 'intermediate position'. The last option is wrong because the radical version meets clear objections.
o: A historical event is described, and then its causes are analyzed.
Two experiments in astronomy are compared, and the more reliable of the two is finally chosen.
A challenge to a traditional view is set out, two forms are distinguished, and a compromise is described.
A theory is introduced and then shown to be accepted by all philosophers.

questions.s: The phrase 'embedded in' in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Galaxies sit inside 'vast halos' of dark matter, so they are surrounded by it. 'Made out of' is tempting, but the passage separates the visible stars and gas from the halo around them.
o: pushed out of
surrounded by
hidden behind
made out of

questions.s: According to paragraph 1, what did the measurements in the 1970s show?
questions.e: Outer stars 'orbit far faster than expected' if only visible stars and gas were present. The planets are a familiar comparison, not the finding, and the passage says dark matter 'neither emits nor absorbs light'.
o: Stars far from a galaxy's center moved faster than visible mass could explain.
Distant planets orbit the Sun more slowly than planets close to it.
Dark matter absorbs the light given off by distant stars.
Spiral galaxies contain much less gas than astronomers had expected to find in their outer regions.

questions.s: Why does the author mention 'distant planets in our solar system'?
questions.e: The phrase 'much as distant planets ... orbit the Sun more slowly' compares the expected pattern for outer stars to a well-known one. The passage does not apply MOND or dark matter to the solar system.
o: To show that MOND also explains the motion of planets
To argue that dark matter is present in our solar system
To explain the method Rubin used to measure the speeds of stars
To give a familiar case of orbital speed falling with distance

questions.s: According to paragraph 3, all of the following are more naturally explained by dark matter EXCEPT:
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says MOND 'predicts the rotation of many individual galaxies with striking accuracy', so this is where MOND does well. The other three options are listed in paragraph 3 as things dark matter explains 'far more naturally'.
o: observations of galaxy clusters
the bending of light by massive objects
the rotation of many individual galaxies
the cosmic microwave background

questions.s: What can be inferred about the failure to detect dark matter particles directly?
questions.e: After this fact the author says 'Each side ... can point to phenomena the other explains less comfortably', so the missing particles help MOND's case. The second option is too extreme; 'so far found none' is not proof.
o: It is one point that supporters of MOND can use in the debate.
It proves that dark matter does not exist in any form.
It explains the pattern seen in the cosmic microwave background.
It shows that MOND cannot work at the scale of galaxy clusters.

questions.s: According to paragraph 1, why was Britain's 1925 decision criticized?
questions.e: Keynes and others 'criticized [it] for overvaluing the pound', which means the rate set the pound's value too high. The first option confuses 1925, when Britain returned to gold, with 1931, when it left.
o: Britain left the gold standard much too early.
It reduced international trade with other countries.
The rate chosen made the pound worth too much.
It brought the era of stable exchange rates to an end.

questions.s: The word 'adherence' in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Economists see 'adherence to gold' as deepening the slump, which matches the evidence that countries that 'held on longer' recovered later; adherence means sticking with it. 'Departure' is the opposite.
o: departure
criticism
uncertainty
continued commitment

questions.s: Why does the author mention France in paragraph 3?
questions.e: France is the example of 'those that held on longer', which 'generally began to recover' later than Britain. The last option reverses the scholars' warning that 'the timing of departure was not random'.
o: To show which country recovered from the slump first
To give an example of a country that kept gold longer and recovered later
To argue that France was the main cause of the Great Depression
To prove that countries left the gold standard at completely random times during the slump

questions.s: The scholars who 'caution' in paragraph 3 would most likely agree that
questions.e: They warn that different circumstances 'complicate any simple inference about cause and effect', so the link alone is not proof. The second option is too extreme: they question the strength of the evidence, not whether gold mattered at all.
o: a link between leaving gold and recovering does not alone prove cause and effect
the gold standard had no effect at all on how deep and how long the slump became
countries chose the time to leave gold without any particular reason
Britain should have stayed on the gold standard after 1931

questions.s: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
questions.e: Paragraphs 2 and 3 present the argument that the system 'helped turn a downturn into the Great Depression', the evidence for it and a caution, ending with most economists' view. The other options are true details, not the main idea.
o: The gold standard promoted stable exchange rates and trade before 1914.
Keynes criticized Britain's decision to return to gold at the prewar rate.
France stayed on the gold standard much longer than Britain did, and it recovered from the slump more slowly.
Many economists think the restored gold standard deepened the Depression, though proof is debated.

questions.s: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 explains how C4 reduces photorespiration, paragraph 2 its many origins, and paragraph 3 the debate about why. The last option is too strong: the passage presents carbon dioxide as one hypothesis that others challenge.
o: C4 plants avoid a weakness of Rubisco, and the trait arose many times for debated reasons.
Maize and sugarcane are the most productive crops grown anywhere in the tropics.
Photorespiration takes place only in tropical grasses growing in hot places.
Falling carbon dioxide alone explains exactly when and where C4 grasslands spread across the world.

questions.s: According to paragraph 1, how do C4 plants reduce photorespiration?
questions.e: C4 plants 'fix carbon in outer leaf cells and then deliver it in concentrated form to inner cells where Rubisco operates'. The first option misplaces Rubisco, which works in the inner cells.
o: They produce extra Rubisco in their outer leaf cells.
They bring concentrated carbon to the cells where Rubisco works.
They grow only in places where temperatures stay low throughout the year.
They remove oxygen from the air around their leaves.

questions.s: The word 'convergent' in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: The trait 'evolved independently more than sixty times in different plant lineages', so many groups arrived at the same solution on their own. 'Extremely rare' contradicts the point that it happened very often.
o: extremely rare
very rapid
reaching the same result separately
slow and gradual

questions.s: All of the following are mentioned as conditions linked to photorespiration or to the spread of C4 plants EXCEPT:
questions.e: Heavy rainfall is never mentioned; in fact, the passage lists 'hot, dry or open habitats'. High temperatures and scarce carbon dioxide make photorespiration worse, and open habitats are linked to C4 expansion.
o: high temperatures
low carbon dioxide
open habitats
heavy rainfall

questions.s: Why does the author mention that C4 grasslands expanded 'millions of years after carbon dioxide had already fallen'?
questions.e: The detail is given by those who 'emphasize hot, dry or open habitats': if carbon dioxide fell long before the expansion, it cannot alone explain when C4 spread. The first option reverses the purpose of the evidence.
o: To support the idea that carbon dioxide alone explains the rise of C4
To give evidence that carbon dioxide may not fully explain the timing
To show that grasses developed C4 before any other plants did
To suggest that carbon dioxide levels were rising at that time

questions.s: What is the passage mainly about?
questions.e: Paragraphs 1 and 2 describe how the beetles 'collect' water from fog, and paragraph 3 explains why 'engineers have studied this design'. The option about fog forming over the Atlantic repeats words from paragraph 1, but the fog is only background to the beetles' behavior. Competition among insects is never discussed.
o: The reasons the Namib Desert receives so little rainfall each year
How certain beetles obtain water from fog and why this interests engineers
The competition among desert insects for the few available sources of water
The way coastal fog forms over the cold waters of the Atlantic Ocean

questions.s: The word 'uniform' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: The next sentences show why the surface is 'not uniform': it has bumps that attract water and waxy areas that repel it. So 'uniform' means the same everywhere. 'Smooth to the touch' is tempting because the surface has bumps, but the contrast in the passage is between two different kinds of area, not about texture alone.
o: attractive
protective
smooth to the touch
the same throughout

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, what happens to the water droplets on the bumps?
questions.e: The passage says droplets 'grow until they become heavy enough to roll down the beetle's back toward its mouth'. The correct option restates this with 'their weight carries them down'. The option about the waxy coating mixes two details: the wax is between the bumps, not on them, and it repels water rather than pushing droplets off the bumps.
o: They gather until their weight carries them down to the beetle's mouth.
They are absorbed directly through the beetle's hard wing covers.
They are pushed away by the waxy coating on the bumps themselves.
They evaporate quickly unless the beetle moves into the shade of a dune.

questions.s: What can be inferred about the timing of fog basking?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 says fog comes 'on many mornings' and that the beetles capture moisture 'before the sun burns the fog away'. So the beetles must act early, before the heat removes the fog. The option about still wind is contradicted by the beetle facing 'the wind', and the desert receives almost no rain at all.
o: It takes place mainly in the late afternoon.
It happens only on days when rain also falls.
It must be done before the fog disappears in the heat.
It is most effective when the wind is completely still.

questions.s: Why does the author mention the mesh nets already used in some coastal villages?
questions.e: The new beetle-inspired nets are made 'in an attempt to improve on the simple mesh nets already used'. The mesh nets are therefore the existing method that engineers hope to do better than. The first option reverses the relationship: the human designs copy the beetle, not the other way around.
o: To show that the beetle's method was copied from human technology
To name a current method that new designs aim to improve
To argue that fog nets work better than any natural surface
To explain why the beetles avoid areas where people live

questions.s: According to paragraph 1, what makes a boulder a glacial erratic?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 describes the boulder as 'made of a type of rock completely different from the bedrock beneath it'. The correct option paraphrases 'bedrock beneath it' as 'the rock underneath it'. The flood option repeats an old explanation that the passage says was later replaced by the ice theory.
o: It is much larger than the other stones near it.
It was left behind by a great flood many thousands of years ago.
Its rock type differs from the rock underneath it.
It is found on a hilltop instead of in a low valley.

questions.s: The word 'plucked' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: The ice 'plucked loose rock from the land and carried it along', so the ice pulled the rock away from where it was. 'Broke down' is tempting because glaciers can wear rock, but the sentence is about lifting and moving rock, not breaking it into pieces.
o: pulled away
broke down
covered up
pressed flat

questions.s: Why does the author mention enormous floods in paragraph 1?
questions.e: Floods are introduced as one of the 'early explanations' for the boulders, and paragraph 2 then presents the ice theory that took its place. Agassiz argued for ice, not floods, so the option about supporting his view reverses the relationship.
o: To describe the force that shaped the bedrock under erratics
To show that floods and glaciers often happened at the same time
To support the view that Louis Agassiz later defended
To give an earlier explanation that was later replaced

questions.s: How is the information in the passage organized?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 presents a puzzle (boulders that 'puzzled observers'), paragraph 2 gives the explanation (movement by ice), and paragraph 3 says erratics 'are valuable evidence'. The option about opposing theories is wrong because the passage clearly accepts the ice explanation.
o: Several kinds of rock are compared according to their age.
A puzzle is described, explained, and then shown to be useful.
Two scientists' opposing theories are presented with no conclusion.
The steps of glacier formation are listed in time order.

questions.s: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about an erratic found very far from its source rock?
questions.e: Researchers 'trace the path that a glacier followed' by linking a boulder to its source, so a boulder far from its source shows that the ice moved a long way. The passage says glaciers carried rocks 'sometimes for hundreds of kilometers', which supports this. The tracing method depends on the mineral makeup staying the same, so that option is wrong.
o: The glacier that carried it traveled a long distance.
It must have been carried by a flood rather than by ice.
Its mineral makeup changed during the journey.
It cannot be traced to any particular bedrock.

questions.s: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
questions.e: The passage explains why the Moon shows one face: Earth's gravity 'slowed the Moon's spin until the bulges stayed pointed at Earth'. The lengthening of Earth's day is true, but it is a minor point in the last paragraph, not the main idea. The dark and light areas are only the observation that introduces the topic.
o: The Moon's surface has dark and light areas that never move.
Jupiter and Saturn have more large moons than the other planets.
Earth's days are steadily becoming longer as a result of the Moon's gravity.
Gravity has slowed the Moon's spin so one side always faces Earth.

questions.s: The word 'them' in paragraph 2 refers to
questions.e: The sentence before says 'these bulges were constantly being pulled out of line', and then 'Earth's gravity tugged on them'. Gravity pulled on the bulges and so acted 'like a brake'. Earth's oceans are never mentioned in the passage.
o: the Moon's months
the bulges
Earth's oceans
the dark areas

questions.s: The word 'gradually' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Gravity worked 'like a brake' and 'gradually slowed' the spin, so the change happened little by little over a long time. 'With great force' is tempting because gravity is a force, but 'gradually' describes the speed of the change, not its strength.
o: suddenly
partly
slowly over time
with great force

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, why did the Moon's rotation stop slowing down?
questions.e: Gravity slowed the spin 'until the bulges stayed pointed at Earth. Once that happened, the slowing stopped.' The correct option paraphrases 'stayed pointed at' as 'stay lined up with'. Jupiter is mentioned only in paragraph 3, for its own moons, so that option mixes two unrelated details.
o: Its bulges came to stay lined up with Earth.
It moved too far away from Earth to be affected.
Its surface became too hard for Earth to stretch.
Jupiter's gravity began to pull in the opposite direction.

questions.s: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT true?
questions.e: Paragraph 3 says the Moon's gravity is 'slowly lengthening Earth's day', so a shorter day reverses the passage. The other three are stated: the equal spin and orbit times (paragraph 1), the moons of Jupiter and Saturn (paragraph 3), and the Moon's faster rotation early in its history (paragraph 2).
o: The Moon spins once in about the same time that it orbits Earth.
Several moons of other planets are tidally locked.
Earth's day is getting shorter because of the Moon.
The Moon probably rotated faster in the distant past.

questions.s: According to paragraph 1, why do trees in the same area have similar ring patterns?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 explains that 'weather affects trees of a species across a region in a similar way', so they share the same pattern. The option about one ring every month contradicts the first sentence, which says trees add 'one growth ring each year'.
o: The same weather influences their growth each year.
They were all planted at the same time by people.
They belong to a species that grows one ring every month.
Their roots share water from a single underground source.

questions.s: The word 'continuous' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Researchers overlap many samples so that the record has no gaps and 'stretches back' year after year; 'continuous' means unbroken. 'Ancient' is tempting because the record goes back thousands of years, but that describes its age, not the fact that it has no breaks.
o: accurate
ancient
unbroken
detailed

questions.s: Why does the author mention living trees in paragraph 2?
questions.e: Living trees are useful because their 'outermost ring is known to belong to the current year'; from this fixed point, researchers match older wood further back. The first option is wrong because dead trees and old timber are exactly what the record is extended with.
o: To show that dead trees cannot be dated by their rings
To explain how researchers give the record a known starting point
To argue that living trees grow faster than older trees did
To describe the forests that provided wood for most ancient buildings

questions.s: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about many other dating methods?
questions.e: Paragraph 3 says other methods 'give a range of possible dates', while tree rings can give 'a precise calendar year'. So these methods generally cannot point to a single year. The option saying they are more precise reverses the comparison.
o: They cannot be used on wooden objects.
They are more precise than tree-ring dating.
They were developed after dendrochronology.
They usually cannot identify one exact year.

questions.s: Which of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 gives the principle (weather produces shared ring patterns), paragraph 2 the method (overlapping samples into a record), and paragraph 3 the use for archaeologists. Other dating methods appear only in one sentence, so the passage does not rank several methods.
o: A problem in archaeology is stated, and two competing solutions are compared.
A historical discovery is described in the order that events happened.
Several dating methods are ranked according to their accuracy.
A principle is explained, then a method based on it, then its use.

questions.s: What is the main topic of the passage?
questions.e: The passage introduces 'a mathematical system for creating the illusion of depth', explains how it was demonstrated and described, and tells how it spread. Brunelleschi is important, but the passage mentions only one thing he did, so it is not about his whole career.
o: The life and career of the architect Filippo Brunelleschi
The development of a method for showing depth in painting
The differences between medieval and modern buildings in Florence
The reasons medieval painters preferred to show large figures

questions.s: Why does the author mention that medieval painters showed important figures larger than less important ones?
questions.e: The next sentence begins with 'however' and describes the new system for creating depth, so the medieval habit is mentioned as a contrast. The passage never says medieval artists lacked mathematical training; that goes beyond what is stated.
o: To contrast an earlier practice with the new realistic method
To explain how Brunelleschi chose which buildings to paint
To show that size was the first rule of linear perspective
To suggest that medieval artists lacked training in mathematics

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, what did Brunelleschi's demonstration show?
questions.e: Brunelleschi showed that 'the painting matched the real scene almost exactly'. The correct option paraphrases this as 'closely matched the actual scene'. The mirror was only a tool for viewing the painting, not a replacement for it, and the vanishing point appears in Alberti's rules rather than in the demonstration.
o: That a mirror could replace painting as a way to record buildings
That viewers preferred paintings of buildings to real buildings
That a vanishing point must always be placed in the center
That his painting closely matched the actual scene

questions.s: The phrase 'credited with' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Brunelleschi is 'usually credited with demonstrating the method', which means people generally give him recognition for it. 'Paid for' is a tempting trap because 'credit' can relate to money, but here the phrase is about who receives recognition.
o: paid for
criticized for
recognized for
taught about

questions.s: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about viewers in the decades after linear perspective spread?
questions.e: Viewers 'came to expect pictures to look like windows onto real space', so paintings that did not create this effect would probably seem less convincing to them. Nothing suggests they lost interest in buildings or wanted grids to end; the grids are what produced the depth they expected.
o: They found pictures without realistic depth less convincing.
They lost interest in paintings that showed buildings, roads, and floors.
They wanted painters to stop using measured grids.
They could not understand Alberti's rules for painters.

questions.s: According to paragraph 1, what do participants in typical experiments do?
questions.e: Participants 'write down as many as they can, in any order'. The first option contradicts 'in any order'. Counting backward is part of the later delay studies in paragraph 3, and it happens after the whole list, not before each word.
o: They repeat a list of words in the exact order that they heard it.
They choose the words they like best from a longer list.
They write down whatever words from a list they can recall.
They count backward before hearing each new word.

questions.s: The word 'These' in paragraph 2 refers to
questions.e: The sentence before introduces 'the last items, called the recency effect', and the next sentence explains why 'These words' are remembered: they are still in short-term memory. The first few words are explained earlier in the paragraph with a different cause, rehearsal into long-term memory.
o: the first few words on the list
new words that arrive
long-term memories
the last items in a list

questions.s: The word 'distinction' in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says the recency effect has 'a different cause' from the primacy effect; paragraph 3 then gives 'evidence for this distinction', that is, for this difference. 'Excellence' is another meaning of 'distinction', but it does not fit a sentence about two causes.
o: difference
discovery
explanation
excellence

questions.s: What can be inferred about a participant who starts writing immediately after hearing a list?
questions.e: The recency effect 'largely disappears' only when there is a delay, because the last words are still 'held in short-term memory when the person starts writing'. With no delay, the last words should still be available. Middle words are the ones remembered worst, so the first option reverses the U-shaped pattern.
o: The participant will recall the words in the middle of the list best.
The participant will likely benefit from the recency effect.
The participant will lose the primacy effect.
The participant will forget the first words on the list.

questions.s: Why does the author mention counting backward for about thirty seconds?
questions.e: Counting backward is introduced as 'evidence for this distinction': it removes the recency effect but leaves the primacy effect, which shows the two have different causes. The option about the primacy effect is reversed, because the primacy effect survives the delay and is linked to long-term memory.
o: To describe a memory exercise that improves recall
To show that the primacy effect depends mainly on short-term memory storage
To explain why the lists used in experiments are short
To describe a test that supports different causes for the two effects

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, which of the following is NOT mentioned as something people did with good coins?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says people 'kept the good ones at home, melted them down, or sent them abroad'. These match the first three options. Paper money is never mentioned in the passage.
o: They stored them in their homes.
They melted them down for the metal.
They sent them to other countries.
They traded them for paper notes.

questions.s: The word 'circulation' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: People spent the damaged coins and kept the good ones, so 'only the poorer coins remained in circulation', that is, in everyday use for buying and selling. 'Storage' is the opposite idea: the good coins were the ones being stored at home.
o: production
storage
general use
official records

questions.s: Why does the author mention a loaf of bread in paragraph 2?
questions.e: The bread is an everyday purchase that 'a full-weight coin and a damaged one could both pay for', which makes concrete the idea of two coins with the same official value. The passage says nothing about bakers refusing coins; in fact the law works because damaged coins were accepted.
o: To show how prices rose when coins were damaged
To give a simple example of two coins with the same legal value
To explain why bakers refused to accept clipped coins
To suggest that food was the main thing people bought in Gresham's time

questions.s: What can be inferred from paragraph 1 about Gresham's law?
questions.e: The passage says 'Gresham was not the first to notice it', so other people must have noticed the principle earlier. The option about Gresham naming it contradicts 'later named Gresham's law' and 'his name became attached to the idea'.
o: Others had observed the idea before Gresham.
Gresham wrote a book that explained it in detail.
The queen rejected Gresham's advice about coins.
It was named by Gresham himself during his lifetime.

questions.s: According to paragraph 3, when can good money stay in use?
questions.e: Paragraph 3 says that 'when people are free to refuse poor coins or to accept them only at a discount, good money can stay in use'. 'At a discount' is paraphrased as 'at lower value'. Fixed official values are the condition that makes the law work, so that option reverses the idea.
o: When coins are made only of gold rather than silver
When people may refuse poor coins or accept them at lower value
When the government sets the same fixed official value for every coin it issues
When damaged coins are melted down and sent abroad

questions.s: What is the passage mainly about?
questions.e: The passage asks why English spelling seems strange and answers with 'the Great Vowel Shift', a set of sound changes, and the fixing of spelling before the shift ended. The printing press is mentioned, but its effect on spelling, not on vocabulary, is a supporting detail.
o: A historical change in pronunciation that helps explain English spelling
The influence of the printing press on the English vocabulary
The reasons that many learners of English find its long vowels so difficult to hear
A comparison of vowel sounds in several European languages

questions.s: The word 'raised' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: The passage defines the word itself: vowels were raised, 'meaning they came to be pronounced with the tongue higher'. 'Made longer' is tempting because the paragraph is about long vowels, but these vowels were already long; what changed was their position.
o: made louder
made higher
made longer
made clearer

questions.s: Why does the author mention the word 'meet' in paragraph 2?
questions.e: 'Meet' follows directly after the statement that most vowels 'were raised', and 'for instance' marks it as an example of that change. The diphthong example is 'time', not 'meet', so the second option mixes up the two examples.
o: To show a word whose spelling changed during the shift
To give an example of a vowel that became a diphthong
To illustrate how a long vowel was raised
To compare the vowels of English and other languages

questions.s: The word 'they' in the sentence 'so they became diphthongs' in paragraph 2 refers to
questions.e: The sentence says 'The two highest long vowels could not rise any further, so they became diphthongs'. The vowels are what changed into diphthongs. 'Combinations of sounds' is the definition of a diphthong, so it describes the result, not what 'they' refers to.
o: learners of English
the new positions in the mouth
combinations of sounds
the two highest long vowels

questions.s: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about English spelling?
questions.e: Spelling became fixed while the shift (1400-1700) was still happening, and words are 'still written the way they were said before the shift was complete'. So spelling often shows older pronunciation. The first option reverses this, since the spellings were based on 'older pronunciations', not new ones.
o: It was invented by printers to match the new pronunciation.
It changed more quickly than pronunciation after the 1470s.
It often reflects how words sounded before about 1700.
It was completely standard before the printing press arrived.

questions.s: According to paragraph 1, which of the following is true of the first Chappe line?
questions.e: The first line linked 'Paris with the northern city of Lille'. The option about any weather is tempting, but paragraph 3 says that is true of the later electrical lines; fog and darkness could stop the Chappe system.
o: It linked Paris with several cities in the south.
It was built after the electrical telegraph.
It connected Paris with a city to the north.
It could carry messages in any type of weather.

questions.s: The word 'relied' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: The system 'relied on a chain of towers', meaning it needed the towers in order to work; it depended on them. 'Focused' does not fit, because the towers were the basic structure of the system, not something it paid attention to.
o: depended
improved
focused
insisted

questions.s: The phrase 'each of which' in paragraph 2 refers to
questions.e: Operators set the beam and arms 'into different positions, each of which stood for a letter, a number, or a whole word'. It is the positions of the arms that carry meaning. The handles are only how operators moved the arms.
o: the towers
the different positions
the operators
the handles

questions.s: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a limitation of the Chappe system?
questions.e: Paragraph 3 lists 'Fog, rain, and darkness' and the need for 'large numbers of trained staff' as limits. The cost of repairing towers is never mentioned, so it is the one option not in the passage.
o: Fog could stop messages from being sent.
It could not be used in the dark.
It needed many trained workers.
Its towers were costly to repair.

questions.s: What can be inferred about why electrical telegraph lines replaced the towers?
questions.e: The towers failed in 'fog, rain, and darkness' because operators had to see the signals, while electrical lines 'worked in any weather'. So the new lines did not need good visibility. The passage never says electrical lines had no operators; that is too extreme.
o: Electrical lines needed no operators at all.
The towers could no longer be seen through telescopes.
Electrical lines did not depend on clear visibility.
The French government wanted to close the Paris line.

questions.s: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
questions.e: The passage centers on the partnership: 'The arrangement benefits both partners.' The option saying scientists agree is wrong because paragraph 3 says the importance of the exchange 'is still debated'. The fungi take sugars, but in return they help the plant, so 'harm' is not supported.
o: Fungi harm many trees by taking sugars from their roots.
Fossils show that plants first grew on land 400 million years ago.
Scientists agree that trees share food through fungal networks.
Plants and fungi form a partnership that helps both of them.

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, why can hyphae absorb resources that roots miss?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 explains that 'hyphae are much thinner than roots', so 'they can reach into tiny spaces between soil particles'. The photosynthesis option reverses the roles: the plant makes sugars, which 'the fungi cannot make for themselves'.
o: They produce their own sugars through photosynthesis.
They are thin enough to enter very small spaces in the soil.
They grow only in soils that are rich in phosphorus.
They connect the roots of several different trees at the same time.

questions.s: The word 'colonize' in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Fungi helped the earliest plants 'colonize land', that is, move onto land and establish themselves there. 'Explore briefly' does not fit, because the plants stayed and spread rather than visiting for a short time.
o: settle in
protect and defend
divide into regions
explore briefly

questions.s: What can be inferred from paragraph 2 about the fungi?
questions.e: The plant gives the fungi sugars 'which the fungi cannot make for themselves', so the fungi rely on plants for this food and energy. This makes the first option unlikely. Hyphae are described as 'much thinner than roots', which contradicts the last option.
o: They could easily survive without any plant partners.
They take water from plants during dry periods.
They depend on plants for a source of energy.
They are larger than the roots of most plants.

questions.s: Why does the author state that the importance of the exchange between trees 'is still debated'?
questions.e: The experiments show that materials 'can move between trees', but how much this matters 'is still debated', so the question is not yet settled. The author does not criticize the experiments or deny that the networks exist; the paragraph begins by describing them in forests.
o: To show that the experiments with carbon were poorly designed
To indicate that some questions about the networks remain open
To argue that mycorrhizal networks are not actually found in real forests
To suggest that trees in natural forests rarely share roots

questions.s: According to paragraph 1, why do sunspots look dark?
questions.e: Sunspots 'appear dark only by comparison' because they are 'more than a thousand degrees Celsius cooler than the surrounding surface'. The option saying they give off no light is contradicted: a sunspot 'would still shine brightly' on its own.
o: They are cooler than the area around them.
They give off no light of any kind.
They are holes that reach deep inside the Sun.
They are covered by clouds of charged particles.

questions.s: Why does the author mention that Schwabe was searching for an unknown planet?
questions.e: Schwabe 'never found the planet, but he noticed' the eleven-year pattern, so his discovery came from work aimed at something else. The passage says he never found the planet, which rules out the second option, and nothing suggests he thought sunspots were planets.
o: To explain why he believed that the dark spots were actually small planets
To show that his search for the planet was successful
To show that his discovery was not what he was looking for
To argue that amateurs should not study the Sun

questions.s: The word 'constant' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: The number of sunspots 'is not constant' because it rises and falls over about eleven years; 'constant' means staying the same. 'Visible' is tempting because the paragraph talks about seeing spots, but the sentence is about change in number.
o: visible
important
accurate
unchanging

questions.s: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in paragraph 3 as something that charged particles from the Sun can affect?
questions.e: Paragraph 3 says the particles 'can also disturb radio communication, satellites, and power grids'. Ocean tides are not mentioned anywhere in the passage.
o: Radio communication
Ocean tides
Satellites
Power grids

questions.s: What can be inferred from the passage about a year of solar maximum?
questions.e: Solar maximum has the most sunspots, and high activity brings 'more solar flares and eruptions of charged particles', which can 'disturb ... satellites'. Auroras come from the same particles, so they should be seen more often, not less.
o: Sunspots will be impossible to observe with a telescope.
The Sun's magnetic fields will be at their weakest.
Auroras will be seen less often than usual.
Satellites may face a greater risk of disturbance.

questions.s: The word 'scarce' in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Pollen survives 'in places where oxygen is scarce', such as the mud at the bottom of lakes, where there is very little oxygen. 'Cold' may describe such places, but it does not explain the meaning of 'scarce', which is about amount.
o: cold
in short supply
poisonous
constantly moving

questions.s: How does paragraph 2 relate to paragraph 1?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 explains how pollen is buried and preserved in lakes and bogs; paragraph 2 describes how palynologists 'drill long cores of sediment from such sites' and identify and count the grains. Paragraph 2 builds on paragraph 1 rather than contradicting it.
o: It gives an example that contradicts the claim in paragraph 1.
It compares the two different kinds of pollen grains mentioned in paragraph 1.
It lists the plants that are mentioned in paragraph 1.
It explains how scientists study the pollen described there.

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, how do palynologists identify the plant a pollen grain came from?
questions.e: Pollen 'can usually be identified by its size, shape, and surface pattern' under a microscope; 'form and surface' paraphrases these features. The depth of a layer tells researchers its age, not which plant the grain came from.
o: By measuring how deep in the sediment core the grain was found
By testing how much oxygen it contains
By examining its form and surface under a microscope
By counting the layers above it in the sediment

questions.s: Why does the author mention a rise in pollen from grasses and cereal crops?
questions.e: The phrase 'for example' introduces this pattern, which 'often marks the moment when early farmers cleared forests'. It illustrates how pollen reveals human activity. The passage does not compare how much pollen grasses and trees produce.
o: To illustrate a pollen pattern linked to early farming
To show that grasses produce more pollen than trees do
To explain why cereal crops were the first plants on land
To argue that forests grew back after farmers left

questions.s: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about pollen evidence?
questions.e: Pollen 'can reveal human activity even at sites where few objects have been found', so it is valuable when artifacts are rare. The option with 'only' is too extreme, since paragraph 2 shows pollen records all kinds of change in vegetation.
o: It can be useful even when a site has few artifacts.
It is less reliable than objects found at a site.
It only shows changes caused by early farmers.
It is most plentiful at the places where people built their homes.

questions.s: What is the passage mainly about?
questions.e: The passage explains how ukiyo-e prints reached Europe, how they differed from European painting, and how painters 'collected these prints and borrowed their ideas'. Trade is only the background in paragraph 1, and carving techniques are never described.
o: The history of trade between Japan and France
The techniques used to carve Japanese woodblocks
How Japanese prints influenced European artists
Why Hokusai and Hiroshige became famous in Japan

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, which feature was typical of the Japanese prints?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says the artists 'used flat areas of bright color'. The shading option describes European painting, which the prints are contrasted with ('Instead of creating deep space ... and shading'). Figures were often 'cut off sharply by the edge', not centered.
o: Careful shading to create deep space
Flat areas of strong color
Subjects taken only from ancient history
Figures placed exactly in the center

questions.s: What can be inferred from paragraph 1 about ukiyo-e prints in Japan?
questions.e: The prints were 'produced cheaply in great quantities for ordinary buyers in Japan', so they were everyday items rather than costly luxuries. The option about foreign traders contradicts 'for ordinary buyers in Japan'.
o: They were not considered expensive luxury objects.
They were made only for sale to foreign traders.
They were banned before Japan opened its ports.
They were produced by European artists living in Japan.

questions.s: Why does the author mention Van Gogh's painted copies of prints by Hiroshige?
questions.e: The paragraph begins by saying painters 'borrowed their ideas', and Degas and Van Gogh are the two examples. Degas and Van Gogh are not contrasted; the word 'while' joins two examples of the same kind of borrowing.
o: To show that Van Gogh preferred copying to original work
To explain how the Japanese prints first arrived in the shops of Paris
To contrast Van Gogh's methods with those of Degas
To give evidence that artists borrowed from Japanese prints

questions.s: The word 'widespread' in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: The fashion was so 'widespread' that it needed its own name, which means it was found among many people; it was common. 'Colorful' describes the prints themselves, not how far the fashion reached.
o: expensive
common
colorful
surprising

questions.s: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT true of the spacing effect?
questions.e: Ebbinghaus used meaningless syllables, but paragraph 2 says the effect has been confirmed 'with many kinds of material, from vocabulary to mathematics', so 'only' makes this option false. The 1880s are in the nineteenth century, and 'learners of all ages' supports the second option.
o: It was first described in the nineteenth century.
It has been found with learners of different ages.
It applies to subjects such as vocabulary and mathematics.
It works only with lists of meaningless syllables.

questions.s: The word 'inefficient' in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Cramming is 'inefficient' because the same study time, if spread out, would produce much longer memory; the long session wastes some of its value. 'Unusual' does not fit, since the passage says students 'often' study this way.
o: wasteful
dangerous
unusual
difficult

questions.s: The phrase 'this effort' in paragraph 2 refers to
questions.e: The sentence says 'the learner must work harder to recall the information', and then 'this effort makes the memory stronger'. The effort is the harder work of recalling. Forgetting is what causes the effort, so the first option confuses cause and result.
o: the forgetting between sessions
the work of recalling the information
the study of mathematics
the proposal of several different explanations

questions.s: According to paragraph 3, why do many learners prefer cramming?
questions.e: Paragraph 3 says 'learners mistake this familiarity for lasting knowledge', so cramming only feels effective. The option about better results on later tests is reversed: 'A test a week later usually shows the difference', meaning cramming does worse.
o: It requires less total study time.
Most teachers recommend it in the days before an important exam.
Familiar material feels like lasting knowledge.
It produces better results on later tests.

questions.s: What can be inferred about a student who crams and is tested one week later?
questions.e: Right after cramming the material 'seems familiar', so the student expects to know it, but a later test 'shows the difference clearly'. The student will likely remember less than he or she believed. 'Completely unfamiliar' goes too far; the passage describes weaker memory, not total loss.
o: The student will probably remember less than expected.
The student will remember more than a student who spaced study.
The student will find the material completely unfamiliar.
The student will have forgotten nothing from the session.

questions.s: According to paragraph 1, which of the following is true of a pidgin?
questions.e: The passage states that a pidgin 'is no one's first language'. A large vocabulary describes a creole, not a pidgin, and speakers 'return to their own languages at home', which rules out the last option.
o: It is not learned as anyone's first language.
It borrows equal numbers of words from many languages.
It has a large vocabulary and complex grammar.
It is spoken mainly at home with family members.

questions.s: The word 'consistent' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Children turn the pidgin into a full language with 'consistent grammar', meaning grammar that follows regular rules. 'Simple' describes the pidgin's grammar before this change, so it is the opposite of the development described.
o: simple
borrowed
difficult
regular

questions.s: Which of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 defines a pidgin, paragraph 2 defines a creole, and paragraph 3 gives Tok Pisin as 'a well-known example'. The passage focuses on one language of Papua New Guinea, not on the history of all the country's languages.
o: Two languages are compared in order to show which is older.
A theory is presented and then shown to be mistaken.
Two terms are defined, and then an example is given.
The history of one country's languages is told in time order.

questions.s: Why does the author mention Tok Pisin in paragraph 3?
questions.e: Tok Pisin 'began as a pidgin' and became 'the first language of many families', which matches the process described in paragraph 2. The passage says Tok Pisin is based on English vocabulary, but it makes no claim about most creoles.
o: To show that pidgins are mainly used for trade
To give a real example of a pidgin that became a creole
To argue that English is the basis of most creoles
To explain why Papua New Guinea has several official languages

questions.s: What can be inferred from the passage about a creole compared with the pidgin it came from?
questions.e: A pidgin is used 'only for limited purposes', while a creole 'can express anything that other languages can', and Tok Pisin is used in newspapers, radio, and parliament. The first option is reversed: a pidgin has no native speakers at all.
o: It has fewer native speakers than the pidgin had.
It is used only for trade between communities.
It can be used for a wider range of purposes.
It takes its vocabulary from several new languages.

questions.s: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
questions.e: The passage presents the longitude problem, explains that it depended on 'keeping accurate time aboard a moving ship', and shows how Harrison's clock 'proved that the time method could succeed'. Latitude and pendulum clocks are true details, but they only support this main point.
o: Sailors found latitude by measuring the height of the Sun.
An accurate sea clock solved the problem of finding longitude.
The British government offered prizes for many inventions.
Pendulum clocks were the most accurate timekeepers of their time.

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, why were pendulum clocks useless at sea?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says 'the rolling of the ship disturbed their swing' and 'changes in temperature and humidity affected their parts'. The correct option sums these up as movement and weather. Size and repairs are never mentioned.
o: They were too large to fit inside a ship's cabin.
They could not show the time at the home port.
The ship's movement and the weather affected them.
Sailors did not know how to repair them on long voyages.

questions.s: Why does the author mention that Earth turns 15 degrees every hour?
questions.e: Because of this rotation, a navigator could 'compare' home-port time with local time 'and calculate how far east or west the ship had traveled'. The fact links a difference in time to a difference in longitude. Latitude is found from the Sun's height, not from time.
o: To explain why long ocean voyages often took many months to complete
To show how latitude is measured
To describe how pendulum clocks were built
To explain how time differences reveal longitude

questions.s: The word 'resembled' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Harrison's fourth clock 'resembled a large pocket watch', meaning it looked like one. 'Was based on' is tempting, but the sentence describes the clock's appearance, not where its design came from.
o: looked like
was smaller than
replaced
was based on

questions.s: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about Harrison?
questions.e: Harrison 'struggled for years to receive full payment', so the reward came slowly and with difficulty. This directly contradicts the option about immediate payment, and nothing suggests he refused the prize.
o: He refused the prize because he wanted no reward.
He was paid the full prize immediately in 1762.
His clocks were used only by the British navy.
The government was slow to reward him fully.

questions.s: The word 'sensible' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: If the gain is small, the costs 'may make it sensible to leave the price unchanged', meaning it is a reasonable, wise choice. 'Required' is too strong; the passage describes a sensible decision, not a rule the firm must follow.
o: obvious
required
pleasant
reasonable

questions.s: Why does the author mention restaurants in paragraph 2?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 opens with 'The name comes from restaurants', which must print new menus when prices change. The author then widens the idea with 'More generally'. Nothing compares how often restaurants and shops change prices.
o: To show that restaurants change prices more often than shops
To explain where the term 'menu costs' comes from
To argue that printing is the largest cost for most firms
To give an example of a business with no changing costs

questions.s: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in paragraph 2 as a menu cost?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 lists 'relabeling goods on shelves, updating catalogs and price lists, reprogramming cash registers, and informing customers'. Training staff is not on the list, so it is the answer.
o: Relabeling goods on shelves
Reprogramming cash registers
Training new sales staff
Updating catalogs and price lists

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, when might a firm decide not to change a price?
questions.e: The passage says that 'if a firm expects only a small gain from adjusting a price, these costs may make it sensible to leave the price unchanged'. The correct option restates this as a gain too small to justify the cost. Competitors are never mentioned.
o: When the gain would be too small to justify the cost
When its customers have asked for lower prices
When its costs have risen sharply in a short time
When competitors have recently printed new menus and catalogs

questions.s: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about online stores?
questions.e: Online shopping makes 'price changes almost free', so menu costs give online sellers little reason to wait, and they can change prices often. Saying they cause sticky prices reverses the idea: they may 'reduce the importance' of menu costs.
o: They print more menus and catalogs than traditional shops.
They never change their prices more than once a year.
They are the main cause of sticky prices today.
They may adjust prices more often than traditional shops.

questions.s: What is the passage mainly about?
questions.e: The passage explains how lodgepole pines 'depend on' fires 'to reproduce': heat opens their cones and the burned ground helps seedlings. The passage says ash 'adds nutrients to the soil', so the option about fire destroying soils contradicts it.
o: How one kind of tree uses fire to help it reproduce
The reasons forest fires have become more common
The ways in which fire destroys forest soils
How ecologists measure the age of lodgepole pines across western North America

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, what causes serotinous cones to open?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says 'the intense heat melts the resin, and the cone scales slowly open'. The first option is contradicted directly: 'Ordinary summer warmth is not enough to open them.'
o: The warmth of an ordinary summer
Animals that remove the resin
The great heat of a fire
Rain that softens the cone scales

questions.s: The word 'intense' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: The heat of a fire is 'intense', unlike 'ordinary summer warmth', so it is extremely strong. 'Sudden' may describe a fire, but the contrast in the paragraph is about how hot it is, not how quickly it arrives.
o: sudden
extreme
brief
natural

questions.s: Why does the author mention that the fire has cleared away competing plants?
questions.e: Paragraph 3 begins 'The timing gives the seedlings important advantages', and the cleared competition is the first of these, followed by the nutrients in the ash. The cones staying closed is explained in paragraph 2 and has nothing to do with competing plants.
o: To show that fires harm young pines
To explain why the cones can stay closed on the branches for many years
To describe how the resin is formed
To explain one advantage seedlings gain from the timing

questions.s: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about a forest that burns again only a few years after a fire?
questions.e: The strategy 'works best when fires are spaced far enough apart for new trees to mature and produce cones of their own'. If a second fire comes too soon, the young trees may not have cones yet, so few seeds would be released. More seedlings is the opposite of what the passage suggests.
o: It will produce more seedlings than after the first fire.
Its soil will contain no nutrients at all.
Its young pines may not yet have cones to release seeds.
Its lodgepole pines will stop producing resin.

questions.s: According to paragraph 1, what is one purpose of color change in many chameleon species?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 says color change is used 'for communication', for example to attract a female or warn a rival, which the correct option calls sending signals. The hiding option repeats the popular belief that the passage corrects, and 'in every situation' is too extreme.
o: Hiding from predators in every situation
Sending signals to other chameleons
Making their skin harder to damage
Finding food in dark places

questions.s: The word 'which' in the phrase 'which in turn changes' in paragraph 2 refers to
questions.e: The animal 'changes the distance between the crystals, which in turn changes which colors of light are reflected'. It is the change in spacing that leads to a change in color. The colors of light are the result, not what 'which' refers to.
o: the outer layer of pigment
the regular pattern
the colors of reflected light
changing the crystal spacing

questions.s: The word 'assumed' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Scientists 'assumed' the pigment explanation until later studies 'pointed to an additional mechanism', so they believed it without full evidence; they supposed it. 'Proved' is wrong because the belief turned out to be incomplete.
o: supposed
proved
denied
measured

questions.s: What can be inferred from paragraph 2 about a chameleon whose crystals move farther apart?
questions.e: When the crystals 'move apart, longer wavelengths such as yellow and red are reflected', so the skin will look more yellow or red. Absorbing heat is linked in paragraph 1 to darker skin, not to the spacing of the crystals.
o: Its skin will absorb more heat from the Sun.
Its pigment grains will disappear.
Its skin will appear more yellow or red.
It will be harder for rivals to see.

questions.s: Why does the author mention butterfly wings and bird feathers?
questions.e: The final sentence says structural color 'is also seen in butterfly wings and bird feathers', giving other cases of the same mechanism. Nothing in the passage suggests a family relationship between chameleons and birds.
o: To point out other animals with structural color
To argue that chameleons are related to birds
To explain how pigment grains move in skin cells
To contrast animals that hide with those that communicate

questions.s: How is the information in the passage organized?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 explains how weak acid dissolves limestone; paragraphs 2 and 3 describe the results: passages, sinkholes and vanishing streams, and the deposits that form stalactites. No theory is rejected, and cave exploration is not discussed.
o: Different types of caves are compared by their size.
A theory about caves is described and then rejected.
A chemical process is explained, followed by its results.
The history of cave exploration is presented in time order.

questions.s: According to paragraph 1, why can rainwater dissolve limestone?
questions.e: Rainwater 'picks up carbon dioxide and becomes a weak acid', and this acidic water dissolves the rock. The second option reverses the passage, which says 'rainwater is rarely pure' and that limestone dissolves only very slowly in pure water.
o: It becomes slightly acidic from carbon dioxide.
It is completely pure when it falls.
It contains large amounts of calcite.
It is heated as it passes slowly through the layers of soil.

questions.s: The word 'seeps' in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: The water 'seeps into cracks' after soaking through soil, so it moves slowly through small openings. 'Rushes' suggests fast movement, which does not fit water passing gradually into narrow cracks.
o: rushes
freezes
falls
slowly flows

questions.s: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a feature of karst landscapes?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 mentions 'passages and chambers', 'sinkholes', and 'streams that suddenly disappear underground'. Hot springs do not appear anywhere in the passage.
o: Sinkholes in the ground
