Hot springs at the surface
Streams that vanish underground
Underground passages and chambers

questions.s: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about the formation of stalactites?
questions.e: Dripping water 'releases some of its carbon dioxide into the cave air' and then 'can no longer hold all of its calcite', which leaves the mineral behind. So stalactites form because the water loses carbon dioxide. Stalactites hang from the ceiling; it is stalagmites that grow on the floor.
o: It happens only in caves that have no air.
It depends on water losing carbon dioxide.
It requires water to be completely pure.
It takes place mainly on the floor of the cave.

questions.s: According to paragraph 1, what makes the Hawaiian Islands unusual?
questions.e: Most volcanoes form near plate edges, but the Hawaiian Islands lie 'thousands of kilometers from the nearest plate boundary'. The option about forming at the edge of two plates reverses this, and the plate moves northwest, not southeast.
o: They contain the tallest volcanoes on Earth.
They are moving toward the southeast.
They formed at the edge of two plates.
They are far from any plate boundary.

questions.s: The word 'it' in the phrase 'it is cut off from its supply of magma' in paragraph 2 refers to
questions.e: The sentence says 'the plate carries the volcano away', and then 'it is cut off from its supply of magma and becomes extinct'. Only a volcano can become extinct. The hot spot stays in place and keeps supplying new volcanoes.
o: the hot spot
the plate
the volcano
the sea floor

questions.s: The word 'striking' in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: The 'striking pattern' is the clear change in age along the island chain, something that stands out and is easy to notice. 'Violent' is tempting because the topic is volcanoes, but the word describes the pattern, not an eruption.
o: violent
noticeable
recent
confusing

questions.s: What can be inferred about the volcanoes on the northwestern islands of the chain?
questions.e: The plate carries volcanoes northwest, away from the hot spot, where they are 'cut off from' magma and become 'extinct'. Only the island of Hawaii, at the southeastern end, 'has active volcanoes'. The islands are 'older toward the northwest', so they are not younger.
o: They are no longer active.
They are younger than those on Hawaii.
They are still growing over the hot spot.
They formed near a plate boundary.

questions.s: Why does the author mention the line of underwater mountains in paragraph 3?
questions.e: After the oldest islands 'have sunk', the chain continues as 'a long line of underwater mountains', so the pattern of ever older volcanoes extends past the islands we can see. The passage presents this as part of what 'the theory explains', so it does not argue against Wilson.
o: To show that the hot spot has recently moved
To describe a different kind of volcano
To show that the pattern continues beyond the visible islands
To argue that Wilson's theory is incorrect

questions.s: What is the main purpose of the passage?
questions.e: The passage begins with the puzzle of Roman structures 'still standing after two thousand years' and then explains the ingredients and chemistry behind this. The author does not reject modern concrete; paragraph 3 notes that Roman concrete could not carry heavy loads.
o: To explain why Roman concrete has lasted so long
To describe the history of harbors near Naples
To argue that modern concrete should no longer be used
To compare the costs of ancient and modern building

questions.s: The word 'exposed' in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Harbor walls 'exposed to seawater for centuries' have been left open to the action of the sea. 'Damaged by' is tempting, but the point of the sentence is that these walls are still standing, so they were not destroyed by the water.
o: hidden from
open to
damaged by
built in

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, what did the volcanic ash do when it was mixed with lime?
questions.e: The ash 'reacted with the lime to form a strong binding material', a material that holds the other parts together. The option about keeping seawater out is contradicted, because seawater did enter and reacted with the ash to form new minerals.
o: It made the mixture lighter so that it could float.
It prevented seawater from entering the concrete.
It reacted to form a material that held the mix together.
It dissolved slowly and left empty spaces behind.

questions.s: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT true of Roman concrete?
questions.e: Paragraph 3 says Roman concrete 'could not support the heavy loads that modern reinforced concrete carries', so the last option reverses the passage. The ingredients, the wooden forms, and the slow gain in strength are all stated.
o: It was made with lime, volcanic ash, and chunks of broken rock.
Some of it was placed in wooden forms in the sea.
It became strong only slowly after it was put in place.
It could carry heavier loads than modern reinforced concrete.

questions.s: What can be inferred from paragraph 2 about cracks in Roman marine concrete?
questions.e: New minerals 'grew in the spaces and cracks', which suggests that cracks were gradually filled in and the material became stronger. The first option contradicts paragraph 1, which says many harbor walls are still standing.
o: They caused most Roman harbor walls to collapse.
They may have been partly filled by new minerals.
They were repaired by Roman workers every year.
They formed only in structures built on land.

questions.s: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
questions.e: The tree gives the ants shelter and food, and 'In return, the ants defend the tree'; the passage calls this a 'partnership'. Belt is mentioned only because Beltian bodies are named after him, so he is a minor detail.
o: Thomas Belt was the first to study ants in Central America.
A tree and ants each provide benefits to the other.
Bullhorn acacias are damaged badly by many kinds of ants.
Ants prefer nectar to every other type of food.

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, what do the ants do with Beltian bodies?
questions.e: The ants 'harvest these structures and feed them to their larvae'; larvae are young ants. The option about storing them in the thorns mixes two details: the ants live in the thorns, but the passage does not say they store food there.
o: They give them to their young as food.
They use them to build their nests.
They store them inside the hollow thorns.
They remove them to protect the leaves.

questions.s: Why does the author mention experiments in which ants were removed from young acacias?
questions.e: The experiments 'showed the value of this protection': without ants, the trees were damaged more and many 'grew slowly or died'. The results show that the ants help the trees, so the first option reverses the finding.
o: To show that the ants harm young trees
To describe how scientists collect and study whole ant colonies
To explain why the trees produce nectar
To provide evidence that the ants' protection matters

questions.s: The word 'aggressively' in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: The ants 'sting and bite insects and even large mammals', which shows that they defend the tree fiercely. 'Carefully' does not match attacks on animals much larger than the ants.
o: carefully
secretly
fiercely
occasionally

questions.s: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about related acacia species?
questions.e: The bullhorn acacia 'lacks much of the chemical defense found in related species', because its ants protect it. This suggests that related species depend more on chemicals to protect themselves. 'Never eaten' is too extreme and is not supported by the passage.
o: They cannot produce nectar or Beltian bodies of any kind.
They grow faster than the bullhorn acacia.
They are never eaten by large mammals.
They probably rely more on chemical defenses.

questions.s: According to paragraph 1, from whom does a young male songbird usually learn its song?
questions.e: A young male learns 'by listening to adult birds, usually his father or other males nearby'. The correct option paraphrases 'males nearby' as 'adult males close by'. Females and other species are not mentioned as teachers.
o: From females of its own species
From birds of other species
From adult males close by
From other young birds

questions.s: Why does the author compare the young bird's practice sounds to the babbling of human infants?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 says bird learning 'resembles, in some ways, the way human children learn to speak', and the babbling comparison is one of those ways. The passage never suggests that birds learn human words, and it does not compare learning speeds.
o: To show that young birds can be taught to copy human speech
To argue that infants learn faster than birds
To explain why birds practice quietly
To point out a similarity in how both learn

questions.s: The word 'model' in the phrase 'the memorized model' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.e: The bird adjusts its sounds 'until it matches the memorized model', the remembered song it is trying to copy. 'Theory' fits a different use of 'model' in the last sentence ('a useful model for studying'), but not this one.
o: example to copy
small toy
fashion
theory

questions.s: What can be inferred from paragraph 2 about birds deafened before the practice stage?
questions.e: The passage says birds 'must hear themselves to compare their attempts with the memory', so deaf birds cannot make this comparison. Nothing suggests they lose the memory itself; the problem is that they cannot hear their own attempts.
o: They forget the song they memorized.
They cannot check their sounds against the memory.
They never begin to practice at all.
They learn a normal song from female birds in the area instead.

questions.s: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT true?
questions.e: Paragraph 3 says a bird that misses adult song in its sensitive period 'never develops a normal version, even if it hears the song later', so the first option is false. The order of memorizing then practicing, the 'weeks of practice', and the 'simplified songs' are all stated.
o: Birds that first hear adult song late still sing normally.
Young birds memorize songs before they begin to practice.
Practice continues for weeks before the song matches the model.
Birds raised without adult song produce simpler songs.

questions.s: What is the passage mainly about?
questions.e: The passage presents Granovetter's finding that "weak ties often matter more" and explains it through network structure, ending with the value of "a wide network of loose connections." The correct option paraphrases weak ties as "loose social connections." The first option reverses the main point, and online platforms are only one brief example in paragraph 3.
o: The reasons close friends are more helpful than acquaintances
An explanation of why loose social connections can be valuable
How online platforms have changed the way people look for work
The methods sociologists use when they interview workers

questions.s: The word "bridges" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Acquaintances "belong to other groups and can act as bridges to news" the inner circle has not heard, so they connect a person to new information. A bridge here is a link between two groups. "Barriers" is the opposite: something that blocks a connection.
o: barriers
rivals
copies
links

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, why do close friends often provide little new information?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says close friends "tend to know one another and move in the same circles, so they usually share the same information." The correct option restates this. The second option describes acquaintances, the people a person sees "only rarely," not close friends.
o: They mostly know the same people and hear the same news.
They rarely see one another and so lose touch with recent news.
They prefer not to share information about jobs with friends.
They usually work in very different professions.

questions.s: What can be inferred about a person who has very few acquaintances?
questions.e: The passage says acquaintances provide "news that a person's inner circle has never heard." Someone with few acquaintances therefore has fewer of these bridges and may not hear such news. The first option reverses this, and nothing suggests that few acquaintances means no close friends.
o: The person will probably find a job faster than others.
The person is unlikely to have any close friends.
The person may miss information that comes from outside their group.
The person tends to rely heavily on online platforms for news about jobs.

questions.s: Why does the author mention "how innovations spread, how rumors travel" in paragraph 3?
questions.e: Paragraph 3 begins "The idea has since been applied far beyond the job market," and these phrases are examples of those new applications. The passage does not compare how harmful rumors and innovations are. Granovetter developed the theory from job interviews, as paragraph 2 explains, so the third option mixes up details.
o: To argue that rumors are more harmful than innovations
To show that the idea has been used to study other topics
To explain how Granovetter first developed his theory
To give examples of problems caused by weak ties in large online networks

questions.s: According to paragraph 1, what was the main limitation of the harpsichord?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 says a harpsichord player "could not easily make individual notes louder or softer" because a pluck sounds the same however hard the key is pressed. The correct option paraphrases this as little control over loudness. The last option repeats the word "quills" but nothing says the sound was too loud.
o: Its strings broke easily when the keys were pressed.
It could only be built by instrument makers in Florence.
Its players had little control over the loudness of each note.
Its quills produced a sound that was far too loud for small rooms.

questions.s: The word "withstand" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Iron frames "could withstand far greater string tension than wooden ones," meaning they could hold up against stronger forces without breaking. "Resist" has this meaning. "Reduce" is tempting, but the frames did not lower the tension; they allowed more of it.
o: resist
measure
reduce
produce

questions.s: The word "them" in paragraph 1 refers to
questions.e: The hammers "struck the strings and then immediately fell back, allowing them to vibrate freely." What vibrates after being struck is the strings. The hammers are tempting because they are the subject of the sentence, but they move away so that the strings can vibrate.
o: the quills
the hammers
the keys
the strings

questions.s: What can be inferred about the word "piano"?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says the original name meant a harpsichord "with soft and loud," which was "shortened to pianoforte, and eventually simply to piano." So "piano" comes from a longer name about volume. Mozart is mentioned only as a composer who wrote for the instrument, not as the person who named it.
o: It was chosen by Mozart to honor Cristofori.
It is a shortened form of a name describing soft and loud playing.
It was first used for harpsichords that had leather hammers.
It became common only after iron frames were introduced in large concert halls.

questions.s: All of the following are mentioned as features of Cristofori's original instrument EXCEPT
questions.e: Paragraph 1 mentions leather-covered hammers that "fell back," and paragraph 2 says touch controlled volume. Cast-iron frames, however, were added "during the nineteenth century," long after Cristofori's invention around 1700. The option about iron frames mixes a later development into the original design.
o: a frame made of cast iron
hammers that were covered in leather
hammers that fell back after striking
changes in volume controlled by touch

questions.s: What is the main purpose of the passage?
questions.e: Paragraphs 1 and 2 explain how soap molecules trap grease, and paragraph 3 describes soap's "weakness" in hard water. The correct option covers both parts. Prices are never discussed, and lye is mentioned only as an ingredient, not as something whose production is described.
o: To compare the prices of traditional soaps and modern synthetic detergents
To describe how lye is produced in factories
To argue that people should avoid washing in hard water
To explain how soap removes oil and why it sometimes works poorly

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, which of the following is true of a micelle?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says the heads face out and "the outside of each micelle is attracted to water." "Drawn to" paraphrases "attracted to." The first option reverses the arrangement: it is the tails that point inward.
o: Its heads point inward toward the oil.
Its outer surface is drawn to water.
It forms only in hard water.
It is made of calcium and magnesium.

questions.s: The word "repelled" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: The tail "is repelled by water but mixes easily with oils," and the word "but" signals a contrast with mixing. Being repelled means being pushed away. "Attracted" is the opposite and is used in the passage for the head.
o: dissolved
attracted
pushed away
covered

questions.s: What can be inferred about washing with ordinary soap in hard water?
questions.e: Paragraph 3 says that in hard water "soap reacts with these minerals to form a sticky scum." Soap that turns into scum is no longer available to clean, so less of it does its job. The option saying washing is impossible is too extreme; the passage calls hard water a "weakness," not a complete failure.
o: Some of the soap is used up reacting with minerals instead of cleaning.
The soap molecules lose their tails and can no longer enter grease.
It removes grease faster because the minerals help micelles form quickly.
It is impossible, because no micelles can form at all.

questions.s: How is the information in paragraph 3 organized?
questions.e: Paragraph 3 first says how soap "is traditionally made," then turns with "However, ordinary soap has a weakness" to explain hard water. The correct option matches this order. The third option is wrong because detergents are offered as an answer to the problem, not rejected.
o: The steps of saponification are listed in time order.
Soap made from fats is compared with soap made from oils.
A problem is presented and then one possible solution to it is rejected.
The making of soap is described, and then a drawback is explained.

questions.s: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
questions.e: The passage explains how wind and the Earth's rotation cause upwelling, which brings nutrients to the surface and supports "a remarkably large share of the world's fish catch." The correct option sums this up. The last option misuses details: the Earth's rotation helps cause upwelling, and El Niño, not the rotation, can reduce fish numbers.
o: Rising water driven by wind makes some coastal seas very productive.
Phytoplankton are the largest living things in the open ocean.
El Niño events are the main cause of nutrient loss in deep water.
Fishing near Peru has declined mainly because of the rotation of the Earth.

questions.s: According to paragraph 1, why does the sunlit layer of the ocean often lack nutrients?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 says nutrients "tend to accumulate in deeper, darker water, where the remains of dead organisms sink and decompose." The correct option paraphrases "accumulate" as "build up" and "decompose" as "breaks down." Fish eating the nutrients is never mentioned.
o: Phytoplankton release nitrates into the air.
Sunlight breaks down phosphates very quickly.
Nutrients build up in deeper water where dead matter breaks down.
Fish living near the surface consume most nutrients before the algae can.

questions.s: The word "slacken" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: The paragraph begins "Upwelling depends on the wind, so it can weaken," and then describes El Niño, when the winds "slacken." Slacken means become weaker or less strong. "Warm" is tempting because warm water is mentioned next, but it describes the water, not the wind.
o: reverse
weaken
strengthen
warm

questions.s: Why does the author mention the anchoveta?
questions.e: Right after saying upwelling regions support "a remarkably large share of the world's fish catch," the author writes "The waters off Peru, for example," and names the anchoveta fishery. It is an example of that productivity. The passage never argues for limits on fishing.
o: To show that small fish are more common than seals
To explain why the Earth's rotation moves surface water
To argue that fishing in upwelling regions should be limited to protect seabirds
To illustrate how productive an upwelling region can be

questions.s: What can be inferred about the waters off Peru during an El Niño event?
questions.e: During El Niño "the winds off South America slacken," and since upwelling "depends on the wind," less cold, nutrient-rich water rises. Fewer nutrients means fewer phytoplankton and fish. The first option reverses the change in the winds, and the second gets the water temperature wrong, since "warm surface water spreads toward the coast."
o: The winds blow harder and push more water offshore.
Cold water covers the coast and stops phytoplankton growth.
Fewer nutrients reach the surface than in normal years.
Seabirds find more food because fish come closer to shore.

questions.s: What is the passage mainly about?
questions.e: The passage describes how the kula worked and ends with Malinowski's conclusion that "economic behavior cannot always be explained by practical need alone." The correct option covers both the system and its lesson. The last option invents a comparison: the passage never says one object was worth more than the other.
o: The dangers of long canoe journeys between islands
A ceremonial exchange system and what it revealed about economic life
The way Malinowski collected shells during his research
Why red necklaces were worth more than white armbands in island markets

questions.s: The word "permanently" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: "No one kept the objects permanently" because each object was eventually passed to another partner. Keeping something permanently means keeping it forever. "Briefly" is the opposite and describes how the objects were actually held.
o: forever
secretly
carefully
briefly

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, where did the value of kula objects come from?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says their value came "from their history, including the famous people who had once held them, and from the reputation a person gained by passing them on generously." The correct option paraphrases "reputation" as "honor." Usefulness is ruled out because the objects "could not be eaten or used."
o: The rare materials from which they were made
Their usefulness as tools and as containers for food
The price they brought in ordinary trade
Who had held them and the honor of passing them on

questions.s: Why does the author mention that the ornaments "could not be eaten or used"?
questions.e: The phrase appears in the outsiders' view that the kula "might seem wasteful," and the next sentence says "Malinowski argued otherwise." So the author sets up an idea in order to challenge it. The last option is wrong because ordinary trade happened "alongside" the kula; the kula itself was ceremonial.
o: To show that the islanders lacked food and tools
To explain why Malinowski stopped studying the kula
To present a view that the passage goes on to challenge
To prove that the kula was a form of ordinary trade in useful goods

questions.s: According to the passage, all of the following are true of the kula EXCEPT
questions.e: The passage states that "No one kept the objects permanently," so the first option contradicts it. The other options are all stated: the objects "traveled in opposite directions," the islands were "spread across hundreds of kilometers of sea," and trade in food and tools "took place alongside" the exchanges.
o: Each participant kept the objects he valued most.
Necklaces and armbands moved in opposite directions.
It linked communities across a wide area of sea.
Practical trade happened at the same time as the exchanges.

questions.s: Why does the author describe conditions in industrial cities and in the countryside in paragraph 1?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 shows that cities had jobs but were unhealthy, while the countryside had space but "few jobs," and then says Howard proposed "a way to combine the advantages of both." The description sets up the problem his idea addressed. The passage does not urge people to stay in villages; Howard wanted a third option.
o: To argue that people should stay in rural villages
To explain why factories moved out of London
To present the problem that Howard's proposal tried to solve
To compare British cities with cities in other countries in the same period

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, how would a garden city grow once it reached its planned size?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says growth "would continue by founding a new garden city nearby rather than by expanding outward." "Starting another garden city close by" paraphrases this. Building on the farmland is wrong because the belt of farmland was meant to be "permanent."
o: By building taller apartment blocks in the center
By turning part of its farmland into new housing
By allowing private landlords to buy more land
By starting another garden city close by

questions.s: The word "collectively" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Land owned "collectively" is contrasted with land held by "private landlords," and its rising value was to benefit all residents. Collectively means jointly, by the group as a whole. "Privately" is the opposite.
o: jointly
privately
cheaply
temporarily

questions.s: What can be inferred about Howard's view of private landlords?
questions.e: Howard planned collective ownership "so that rising land values would benefit residents rather than private landlords." This implies he did not want landlords to gain from those rising values. The passage gives no role to landlords in designing or paying for the towns.
o: He believed they were best suited to design new towns.
He wanted to keep them from profiting as land values rose.
He expected them to pay for the central gardens.
He thought they would move to the countryside once garden cities were built.

questions.s: All of the following are features of Howard's garden city EXCEPT
questions.e: Paragraph 2 mentions a "central garden," a "permanent belt of farmland" and a "limited population." It rejects outward growth: new growth would come from a new city "rather than by expanding outward." So steady outward growth is not a feature of the plan.
o: a garden at its center
a permanent belt of farmland
a population limit
steady outward growth

questions.s: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
questions.e: The passage says development "proceeds partly by elimination" and explains how and when synapses are pruned. The correct option captures both the forming and the removing of connections. The first option reverses the passage, which says a young child has "far more synapses than an adult" in some regions.
o: Adults have many more synapses than young children in every region of the brain.
Microglia are the main cause of poor judgment in teenagers.
The brain stops changing once a child reaches school age.
Brain development involves removing connections as well as forming them.

questions.s: The word "engulfing" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Microglia help remove "unwanted synapses" by engulfing them, that is, by surrounding and taking them in. "Swallowing up" has this meaning. "Repairing" does not fit, because the synapses are being eliminated, not fixed.
o: repairing
connecting
swallowing up
counting

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, which connections are most likely to be kept?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says "Connections that are used often tend to be strengthened and kept." "Frequently active" paraphrases "used often." Vision and hearing are mentioned in paragraph 3 only to describe when pruning happens, not which connections survive.
o: Those formed most recently
Those that are frequently active
Those located near microglia
Those that carry information about vision and hearing

questions.s: What can be inferred from paragraph 2 about two children who have very different experiences?
questions.e: Because pruning keeps connections that are used and the network is "shaped by the experiences a child actually has," different experiences should lead to somewhat different networks. The last option is too extreme: pruning happens in every developing brain, not only in some children.
o: Their brain networks may be pruned in somewhat different ways.
They will have exactly the same number of synapses as adults.
Their microglia will stop working before the teenage years.
Only the child with more experiences will undergo pruning at all.

questions.s: Why does the author mention the prefrontal cortex in paragraph 3?
questions.e: Paragraph 3 contrasts early-refined areas for vision and hearing with the prefrontal cortex, which "continues to be pruned into the teenage years and beyond." It is an example of late pruning. The first option reverses this point.
o: To show that pruning ends in early childhood
To explain how microglia were first discovered
To give an example of a region that is refined late
To argue that vision matters more than planning and self-control

questions.s: How is the passage organized?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 gives the potato's origin in the Andes, paragraph 2 describes European suspicion and efforts to overcome it, and paragraph 3 explains why it was finally adopted. The correct option follows this order. Wheat and rye appear in only one comparison, so they do not organize the passage.
o: It traces the potato from its origin through early resistance to acceptance.
It compares the potato with wheat and rye in several different regions of Europe.
It describes a problem with potato farming and then offers a solution.
It lists the poisonous plants that are related to the potato.

questions.s: The word "suspicious" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Europeans were suspicious because the potato was related to "poisonous species" and seen as food "fit only for animals." Being suspicious means being distrustful. "Curious" suggests interest, which does not match the negative attitudes described.
o: curious
distrustful
unaware
envious

questions.s: The word "Their" in paragraph 3 refers to
questions.e: Paragraph 3 begins "Their efforts were eventually rewarded," right after the description of how Frederick the Great and Parmentier promoted the potato. The efforts belong to these rulers and reformers. The peasants were the people being encouraged, not the ones making the efforts.
o: suspicious Europeans
poisonous species
Frederick the Great and Parmentier
the peasants who were asked to plant potatoes

questions.s: According to the passage, all of the following were advantages of the potato EXCEPT
questions.e: Paragraph 3 lists the potato's success in "cool, damp climates," its high calories and its long storage. Paragraph 2, however, says its "green leaves and sprouts do contain toxic compounds," so the leaves were not safe to eat. That option contradicts the passage.
o: It grew well in cool and damp weather.
It yielded many calories per field.
It could be kept in the ground for months.
Its leaves could be eaten safely.

questions.s: What does the phrase "Some historians argue" in paragraph 3 suggest about the claim that follows?
questions.e: "Some historians argue" presents the claim as the view of certain experts rather than as an established fact. This suggests not everyone agrees. Nothing in the passage says the claim has been disproved, and it refers to "much of Europe," not only France.
o: It has been shown to be false by more recent research on population.
It is supported by some experts but is not universally accepted.
It was first made by Frederick the Great.
It applies only to France and not to the rest of Europe.

questions.s: What is the main purpose of the passage?
questions.e: Most of the passage explains how chromium forms a thin oxide film that "seals" stainless steel off from air and water and even re-forms after scratches. The correct option states this purpose. Molybdenum is only one detail in paragraph 3, and cost is mentioned only in passing for ordinary steel.
o: To compare the cost of ordinary steel with that of stainless steel
To describe how molybdenum is added to steel used near the sea
To explain how a thin surface layer protects stainless steel
To argue that ordinary steel should no longer be used in kitchens

questions.s: The word "clings" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: The film "clings tightly to the metal," in contrast to rust, which is "loose and flaky" and breaks away. To cling is to stick firmly. "Spreads" is tempting, but the point is how firmly the layer holds on, not how far it extends.
o: melts
sticks
fades
spreads

questions.s: According to paragraph 1, why does rust allow ordinary steel to keep corroding?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 says rust "tends to break away from the surface, exposing fresh metal underneath to further attack." The correct option paraphrases "break away" as "falls away." Being transparent is a property of chromium oxide in paragraph 2, not of rust.
o: It attracts more moisture than clean iron does.
It contains carbon that reacts with oxygen.
It turns transparent and cannot be seen.
It falls away and leaves new metal exposed.

questions.s: What can be inferred from paragraph 2 about how a scratched stainless steel surface repairs itself?
questions.e: After a scratch, "the exposed chromium quickly reacts with oxygen in the air and the protective layer forms again." Since the repair is a reaction with oxygen, it must depend on oxygen being available. The last option contradicts the word "quickly."
o: It depends on oxygen being present around the metal.
It requires the object to be coated with molybdenum.
It happens only in steel with more carbon than iron.
It takes many years because the layer grows very slowly.

questions.s: All of the following are mentioned as properties of the chromium oxide layer EXCEPT
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says the layer is "a few billionths of a meter thick," "completely transparent," and "forms again" after a scratch. The reddish-brown color belongs to rust, the iron oxide of paragraph 1. That option mixes up the two oxides.
o: It gives the metal a reddish color.
It is only billionths of a meter thick.
It cannot be seen because it is clear.
It can form again after being damaged.

questions.s: What is the passage mainly about?
questions.e: The passage explains how a returning worker's dance communicates the direction and distance of flowers to other workers. The correct option summarizes this. Von Frisch's prize is a supporting detail in paragraph 1, and scent is mentioned as a clue to the flowers, not as a defense.
o: The reasons honeybees prefer certain kinds of flowers over others
How von Frisch won the Nobel Prize
The way bees use scent to defend the hive
How honeybees tell one another where food can be found

questions.s: The word "encodes" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: The direction of the run "encodes the direction of the food," and the passage then explains how an angle on the comb stands for an angle from the sun. To encode something here is to represent it with a signal. "Hides" is wrong because the dance is meant to share information, not conceal it.
o: represents
hides
changes
follows

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, what does a longer waggle run indicate?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says "The length of each waggle run signals distance, with longer runs indicating more distant flowers." The correct option restates "more distant" as "farther." The sun is linked to the direction of the run, not to its length.
o: The flowers are closer to the sun.
The dancer has collected more nectar.
The food is farther from the hive.
The other bees should leave at once.

questions.s: Based on paragraph 2, a bee whose waggle run points straight down the comb is most likely indicating food located
questions.e: A run "straight up the comb means 'fly toward the sun,'" and angles to the right of vertical mean angles to the right of the sun. A run pointing straight down is the reverse of straight up, so it indicates the direction away from the sun. "Directly toward the sun" reverses the relationship.
o: directly toward the sun
in the direction opposite the sun
very close to the hive
40 degrees to the right of the sun

questions.s: Why does the author mention that "the hive is dark"?
questions.e: The sentence reads "Because the hive is dark, the bee uses gravity as a reference," so the darkness explains why gravity, rather than the sun itself, is used for direction. The passage does not say scent replaces dancing; scent is an extra clue.
o: To show that bees cannot see the flowers they describe
To explain why bees rely mainly on scent rather than on dancing
To explain why the dancing bee uses gravity as its guide
To suggest that von Frisch found it difficult to observe the bees inside the hive

questions.s: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
questions.e: The passage presents Veblen's idea that people buy visible goods "for social standing" rather than for usefulness, and then shows its lasting influence. The correct option paraphrases "conspicuous consumption." The third option reverses the idea of Veblen goods, whose appeal "can actually increase as their price rises."
o: Wealthy people in 1899 owned more silver than people do today.
Veblen argued that people often spend money to display their social position.
Economists have proven that luxury goods always lose their appeal as their prices rise.
Ordinary families should avoid imitating the spending of the rich.

questions.s: The word "anonymous" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: In an anonymous society "people cannot easily judge one another's wealth directly" because they do not know each other personally. "Impersonal" fits this meaning. "Crowded" is tempting because the society is "large," but anonymous describes the lack of personal knowledge, not the number of people.
o: wealthy
crowded
modern
impersonal

questions.s: Why does the author mention a handmade silver spoon in paragraph 1?
questions.e: The spoon "stirs food no better than a cheap one; its real function is to show that its owner can afford to spend money." It is an example of buying for display. The second option reverses the point, since the spoon works no better than a cheap one.
o: To illustrate an object valued more for display than for use
To show that silver spoons work better than cheap ones
To explain how Veblen himself earned his wealth
To describe a common gift given at weddings among the wealthy

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, why do people rely on visible signs of wealth?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says that in a large society "people cannot easily judge one another's wealth directly, so they rely on visible signs." The correct option restates this cause. No laws are mentioned, and housing and entertainment are both listed as signs, not compared.
o: Laws require the rich to show their wealth in public.
Ordinary families cannot afford to buy fine clothing or very large houses.
In large societies, it is hard to tell directly how rich others are.
Wealthy people prefer entertainment to housing.

questions.s: What can be inferred about a Veblen good?
questions.e: For Veblen goods, "a high price is part of what makes them impressive," so lowering the price could reduce their appeal. The first option reverses this relationship. The passage calls them "luxury items," not practical tools.
o: It usually sells much better when its price is lowered sharply.
It is usually a practical item such as a tool.
It is bought mainly by people who lack education.
A lower price might make it less attractive to buyers.

questions.s: Which of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 explains that neumes "did not indicate exact pitches," and paragraphs 2 and 3 describe Guido's lines and syllables, which "helped solve this problem." The correct option follows this order. The modern classroom is mentioned only at the end, so the passage does not begin with it.
o: A limitation of an early system is described, and then later improvements.
Two rival teachers are compared, and the more successful one is identified.
A modern classroom practice is explained and then traced back to its origin.
Several kinds of chant are listed in order from oldest to newest.

questions.s: The word "repertoire" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Singers learned "a large repertoire of chants," meaning the whole body of pieces they could perform. "Collection of works" matches. "Audience" is wrong because the repertoire is made up of chants, not listeners.
o: audience
instrument
collection of works
set of rules

questions.s: According to paragraph 1, what was the main limitation of neumes?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 says neumes showed whether a melody rose or fell, "but they did not indicate exact pitches." "Precise" paraphrases "exact." The third option is wrong because neumes were written "above the words."
o: They could be read only by scribes.
They did not show precise pitches.
They were written below the words.
They were too difficult to memorize.

questions.s: What can be inferred about singers before Guido's system came into use?
questions.e: Neumes were only "reminders for singers who already knew the tune," and Guido's system let a singer perform a melody "without having heard it before" for the first time. This implies earlier singers had to hear a melody first. The third option reverses Guido's claim that learning used to take "many years."
o: They could not sing melodies that rose or fell.
They refused to use any kind of written marks above the words of a chant.
They learned new chants more quickly than later singers.
They generally needed to hear a melody before they could sing it.

questions.s: Why does the author mention "the do, re, mi still used in classrooms today"?
questions.e: The author says Guido's syllables "are the ancestors of the do, re, mi still used in classrooms today," which shows that his method still has influence. The last option contradicts this, since the syllables are still in use. Nothing is said about how often the hymn is sung now.
o: To show that the hymn Guido used is still widely sung
To point out a lasting effect of Guido's teaching method
To explain why colored lines were used for certain notes
To argue that modern teachers have abandoned Guido's syllables entirely

questions.s: What is the passage mainly about?
questions.e: The passage explains what the Maillard reaction is, why it needs high temperatures, and how it differs from caramelization. The correct option summarizes this as a "heat-driven reaction" behind browning and flavor. Maillard himself is mentioned only because the reaction is named after him.
o: The life and career of Louis-Camille Maillard
A heat-driven reaction that gives many cooked foods their color and flavor
Methods for preventing roasted coffee from losing its aroma
The reasons caramelization matters more than other processes in cooking

questions.s: The word "dramatically" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: The reaction "proceeds slowly" at ordinary temperatures but "speeds up dramatically" at 140 degrees, a strong contrast. Dramatically here means sharply or by a large amount. "Gradually" is the opposite of the sudden change described.
o: slightly
gradually
dangerously
sharply

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, why do boiled foods rarely brown?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says that "as long as water is present, the surface of the food cannot rise much above 100 degrees," while fast browning needs about 140 degrees. The correct option paraphrases this. Caramelization needs "even higher temperatures," so boiling cannot cause it either.
o: Boiling removes the amino acids from the food.
Sugars dissolve completely in boiling water.
Water keeps the surface temperature too low.
Boiling causes caramelization instead.

questions.s: Why does the author mention that cooks "pat meat dry before searing it"?
questions.e: The sentence begins with "therefore," linking it to the fact that water keeps food below 100 degrees. Drying the meat removes water so the surface can get hot enough to brown, which is a practical application. Crowded pans are a problem because they trap steam, not because they are unsafe.
o: To give a practical use of the point about temperature
To show that dry meat contains more amino acids than wet meat
To explain the difference between searing and caramelization
To warn readers that crowded pans can be unsafe

questions.s: According to the passage, all of the following are true of caramelization EXCEPT
questions.e: Paragraph 3 says caramelization "involves sugars alone," so it does not need amino acids; those are part of the Maillard reaction. The passage does state that caramelization produces brown color, needs "even higher temperatures," and often happens together with the Maillard reaction.
o: It can produce a brown color.
It often occurs together with the Maillard reaction.
It requires amino acids from proteins.
It usually needs higher temperatures than the Maillard reaction.

questions.s: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
questions.e: The passage explains that the deep ocean's circulation "depends on density," which comes from temperature and salt, and describes how this water sinks and travels. The correct option sums this up. The third option is too strong: scientists are only "studying whether" melting ice could slow the system.
o: Winds are the most important force in every part of the ocean.
Sea ice prevents polar water from sinking to the sea floor.
Scientists have proven that melting ice has already stopped the ocean's conveyor.
Differences in density drive a slow circulation of deep ocean water.

questions.s: The word "frigid" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Surface water "loses heat to the frigid air" in polar regions, so the air must be much colder than the water. Frigid means extremely cold. "Very dry" does not explain why the water would lose heat.
o: extremely cold
very dry
fast-moving
polluted

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, how does the formation of sea ice affect the nearby water?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says that when sea ice forms, "it leaves much of its salt behind in the surrounding water," so that water becomes saltier. The option about adding fresh water reverses this; fresh water from melting ice is a separate idea in paragraph 3.
o: It makes the water warmer and lighter.
It increases the water's salt content.
It adds fresh water that floats on top.
It pushes the water toward the equator.

questions.s: The word "it" in the sentence "From there it spreads slowly through the ocean basins" refers to
questions.e: The sentence before says the cold, salty water is dense enough "to sink thousands of meters to the sea floor," and "From there" means from the sea floor. What spreads from there is that dense water. The sea floor is the place it starts from, not the thing that moves.
o: the sea ice
the frigid air
the cold, salty water
the floor of the deep ocean

questions.s: What can be inferred about the possible effect of large amounts of fresh water from melting ice?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 says "salty water is denser than fresh water," and sinking needs water that is "both cold and salty." Adding fresh water would lower the salt content and density, which explains why it might slow the sinking. The last option contradicts the passage, which names salt as one of the two factors.
o: It could make polar surface water less dense and less likely to sink.
It would make the water saltier and speed up the conveyor.
It would mainly affect the winds that drive surface currents.
It could have no effect, since only temperature affects the density of seawater.

questions.s: What is the main purpose of the passage?
questions.e: The passage introduces Hall's idea of proxemics, describes his four zones, and explains how they vary by culture. The correct option states this purpose. The first option is too extreme: closeness is normal in the intimate and personal zones, and its meaning depends on the relationship and culture.
o: To argue that standing close to others is always impolite
To compare the lectures of several American anthropologists
To describe a theory about how people use space when they communicate
To explain why business meetings should be held at a public distance in every culture

questions.s: The word "intrusive" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: A distance that seems "warm and friendly" in one society may feel intrusive in another, so intrusive is the negative opposite: entering someone's space in an unwelcome way. "Distant" is tempting but means too far away, while intrusive suggests coming too close.
o: generous
unwelcome
distant
formal

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, what distance is typical of conversations between friends?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says "Personal distance, extending to a little over a meter, is typical of conversations between friends." Less than half a meter is intimate distance, which is for close family and partners, and one to three and a half meters is the social distance used in business.
o: Up to a little over a meter
Less than half a meter
From one to three and a half meters
More than three and a half meters

questions.s: What can be inferred about a person who steps back when a stranger stands very close?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says that when someone enters a zone "that the situation does not call for, people often feel uncomfortable and step back, sometimes without realizing it." A stranger standing very close is such a case. The third option is wrong because the reaction is often unconscious, not planned.
o: The person is trying to start a business conversation.
The person wants to show respect by giving a speech.
The person has carefully planned to appear cold and unfriendly toward the stranger.
The person may be reacting to an unexpected entry into a closer zone.

questions.s: Why does the author mention that Hall's zones were "based largely on observations of middle-class Americans"?
questions.e: The detail prepares for paragraph 3, where Hall stresses that "the exact boundaries differ across cultures." Saying the numbers come from one group signals that other groups may differ. The third option is too extreme; the passage never ranks Americans against all other cultures.
o: To show that Hall never traveled outside the United States
To indicate that the distances may not apply to every group
To prove that Americans prefer larger distances than all other people
To explain why public distance is used for lectures

questions.s: What is the passage mainly about?
questions.e: The passage describes how New Caledonian crows make hooks and leaf tools in the wild and what laboratory studies reveal about how they learn. The correct option covers this. Chimpanzees appear only in one sentence of paragraph 1 and are never compared with crows in captivity.
o: The skill with which a species of crow makes and uses tools
The differences between chimpanzees and crows in captivity
The types of insects that live inside dead wood
How pandanus plants protect themselves from birds

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, how do the crows use pandanus leaves?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says a crow may "cut a narrow strip with a tapered, saw-toothed edge from the tough leaves of the pandanus plant" and poke it into a hole. The correct option paraphrases this. The last option repeats the words "holes" and "wood" but describes something the passage never mentions.
o: They eat the leaves when larvae are hard to find.
They weave the leaves into nests on dead trees.
They cut strips from them to make probing tools.
They use the leaves to cover holes in the wood.

questions.s: What does the author suggest by noting that the shapes of pandanus tools "differ from one part of the islands to another"?
questions.e: The passage says these differences have "led some researchers to suggest that the designs are passed on socially, much like local traditions." Learning from other crows nearby is what "passed on socially" means. Nothing suggests the plants themselves differ in shape or that some crows cannot make tools.
o: The pandanus plants themselves grow in very different shapes in each area.
Crows in some areas are unable to make tools.
Researchers have measured the tools incorrectly.
Crows may learn tool designs from others in their area.

questions.s: The word "refine" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Young crows already have a partly inborn ability, and watching their parents "likely helps them refine their technique," that is, make it better. "Improve" fits. "Abandon" would mean giving the technique up, which is the opposite.
o: abandon
improve
explain
hide

questions.s: All of the following are mentioned as evidence about how crows acquire their tool skills EXCEPT
questions.e: The passage mentions hand-raised young crows that still probe, juveniles watching their parents, and regional differences in tool design. It never says adult crows punish young birds. That option is not mentioned anywhere in the passage.
o: Young crows raised without adults still probe with twigs.
Juveniles watch their parents for a long time.
Tool designs vary from region to region.
Adult crows punish young birds that use tools poorly.

questions.s: Which of the following best describes the main purpose of the passage?
questions.e: Paragraphs 1 and 2 describe Jacobs's challenge to the planning "orthodoxy" of her time, and paragraph 3 adds that critics say she "underestimated economic pressures." The correct option covers both the critique and its limitation. The last option overstates one detail: her lack of training is mentioned, but the passage draws no general conclusion from it.
o: To praise Le Corbusier's influence on modern housing design
To explain why superblocks reduced crime in American cities
To present a critique of mid-century planning and note a limitation of it
To argue that formal training is unnecessary for anyone who designs cities

questions.s: The word "orthodoxy" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Jacobs "challenged this orthodoxy," referring to the views that "influential planners" shared at the time. An orthodoxy is a generally accepted set of beliefs, or doctrine. "Building method" is tempting because the planners' ideas involved buildings, but the word refers to their shared beliefs, not a technique.
o: accepted doctrine
careful research
local government
building method

questions.s: It can be inferred from paragraph 2 that Jacobs would most likely object to
questions.e: Jacobs valued streets "lined with shops, homes, and workplaces" that draw people "at different hours." A housing estate cut off from shops and workplaces would lack this mix and the "eyes on the street" it provides. The other three options describe features she praised, such as old and new buildings and short blocks.
o: a street on which small cafés and shops stay open well into the evening
a neighborhood containing both old and new buildings
a district with short blocks and many small shops
a housing estate separated from all shops and workplaces

questions.s: Why does the author mention that Jacobs had "no formal training in planning"?
questions.e: The detail contrasts Jacobs with the "influential planners" whose orthodoxy she challenged, highlighting that the criticism came from an outsider. The passage never questions the basis of her ideas; it says they are now "widely accepted." It also says they once seemed "radical," so they were not adopted immediately.
o: To suggest that her ideas lacked any factual basis
To emphasize that her challenge came from outside the profession
To explain why planners immediately adopted her proposals
To show that Le Corbusier also lacked formal training in architecture

questions.s: What is the function of the final sentence of the passage?
questions.e: The sentence begins with "Yet some critics contend" and argues that Jacobs "underestimated economic pressures," which is a reservation, or doubt, about her analysis. It does not add support for her views on safety. The radical nature of her ideas is mentioned in the sentence before, not explained in this one.
o: It introduces a reservation about Jacobs's analysis.
It provides further evidence that her ideas improve safety.
It explains why her ideas were once considered radical.
It describes how modernist planners responded to her book.

questions.s: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
questions.e: The passage opens by calling localization one of the most "persistently" debated questions, then presents evidence for it (Broca, Wernicke) and against it (Lashley), ending with a middle position. The correct option captures this ongoing disagreement. The third option is too strong: Lashley offered a different view of memory but did not prove Broca wrong.
o: Phrenology was the first scientific theory of brain function to be widely accepted.
Researchers have long disagreed about how far brain functions are localized.
Lashley proved that Broca's observations of patients were incorrect.
Language is controlled entirely by one small region of the left frontal lobe.

questions.s: The word "durable" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Phrenology's method "was soon discredited, but the underlying intuition" proved more durable, meaning it survived much longer. "Lasting" matches. "Popular" is tempting, but the contrast with "soon discredited" is about how long the idea endured, not how many people liked it.
o: fragile
popular
obvious
lasting

questions.s: What can be inferred about the patients Wernicke described?
questions.e: Broca's patient "could understand speech but produce almost none," and Wernicke's patients showed "the opposite pattern" with "fluent but largely meaningless speech." The opposite of Broca's case is easy speech with poor understanding. The second option describes Broca's patient, and the damage was "farther back," not in the same area.
o: They had difficulty understanding language, though they spoke easily.
They could understand speech but produce almost none.
They had damage in exactly the same area as Broca's patient.
They were trained in mazes before their brains were studied in detail.

questions.s: According to paragraph 3, what did Lashley conclude from his experiments?
questions.e: Lashley proposed "that memory is distributed broadly across the cortex," because performance depended on how much tissue was removed rather than where. The correct option paraphrases "distributed broadly" as "spread widely." The first option reverses his conclusion and states the localization view he doubted.
o: Each memory is stored in one specific area of the cortex.
Rats learn mazes more slowly than other animals do.
Memory is spread widely over the cortex rather than located in one spot.
Removing the frontal lobe affects speech more than any other kind of damage.

questions.s: Why does the author mention phrenology in paragraph 1?
questions.e: Phrenology's "method was soon discredited," but its "underlying intuition" of specialized regions "proved more durable" and was later supported by Broca. So the author uses it to introduce a flawed early form of the localization idea. The third option is wrong because the passage says the intuition survived and gained strong support.
o: To show that skull shape is a reliable guide to personality
To describe the method Broca used to study his patient
To argue that the idea of specialized brain regions has no scientific value at all
To introduce an early, flawed version of an idea that later gained support

questions.s: Which of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 ends with a question, "why did people adopt it?", and paragraphs 2 and 3 review Childe's climate idea, demographic pressure, and the feasting hypothesis. The correct option fits this structure. The third option reverses the passage, which questions the common belief that farming was "an obvious improvement" rather than defending it.
o: A historical event is described, and its causes are listed in order of importance.
Two archaeologists' careers are compared, and one is judged more successful.
A common belief is defended against several criticisms in turn.
A puzzle is raised, and several competing explanations are then reviewed.

questions.s: The word "compelled" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Under demographic pressure, foragers "may have been compelled to extract more food from less land, even at the cost of harder work," which describes something done out of necessity. "Forced" matches. "Persuaded" is tempting, but it suggests being convinced by argument, not being driven by circumstances.
o: permitted
forced
persuaded
inspired

questions.s: Why does the author mention that early farmers were shorter and suffered more tooth decay?
questions.e: The passage says farming "is often portrayed as an obvious improvement" and then that "Skeletal evidence complicates that picture." The health details are that evidence, so they challenge the idea that farming was clearly better. They have nothing to do with Childe's climate theory, which appears in the next paragraph.
o: To show that foragers ate mainly grain
To support Childe's claim about climate change
To challenge the view that farming was clearly beneficial
To explain why Göbekli Tepe was built by hunter-gatherers rather than farmers

questions.s: According to the passage, what weakened Childe's explanation?
questions.e: After describing Childe's idea of a drying climate, the passage says "Later research, however, found little evidence of such widespread drying." The correct option paraphrases this. Monumental sites are used to support the feasting hypothesis, not to argue against Childe.
o: Researchers found little sign of the climate change it assumed.
Populations at the time were shrinking rather than growing.
Domesticated animals did not need water to survive.
Hunter-gatherers had already built monumental sites in several regions.

questions.s: What can be inferred about supporters of the feasting hypothesis?
questions.e: The hypothesis "shifts attention from necessity to ambition" and links farming to individuals "seeking prestige" through "communal events," which are social motives. The first option reverses this by stressing necessity. The last option is too strong, since the passage calls the proposal "contested."
o: They believe hunger was the main reason people began farming.
They deny that Göbekli Tepe was built by hunter-gatherers.
They regard social motives as a possible driver of early farming.
They consider the hypothesis fully proven by the skeletal evidence from early farms.

questions.s: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
questions.e: The passage explains that glass is an "amorphous solid" without long-range order and then corrects the "persistent myth" that it flows. The correct option links the structure to the misconception. The third option states the myth itself, which the passage rejects.
o: Glass is a disordered solid, a fact that has fed a popular misconception.
Glass and quartz have identical atomic structures because both contain silica.
Glass slowly flows at room temperature, which explains the shape of old windows.
Ice and glass become solid in the same way when they are cooled.

questions.s: The word "abruptly" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Ice solidifies "abruptly at a fixed melting point," in contrast to glass, which hardens "steadily" over "a range of temperatures." The contrast with a gradual change shows that abruptly means suddenly. "Completely" does not fit the contrast, because both materials end up fully rigid.
o: completely
permanently
suddenly
partially

questions.s: According to paragraph 1, how does the arrangement of atoms in glass differ from that in quartz?
questions.e: In quartz, atoms form "a regular pattern that repeats over long distances," while in glass they "lack this long-range order." The correct option restates this difference. The third option is wrong because the atoms in glass are "locked in place"; glass only resembles a frozen snapshot of a liquid. The last option reverses the two materials.
o: Glass contains no silica at all.
Its atoms do not form a pattern that repeats over long distances.
Its atoms move freely, as they do in a liquid.
Quartz atoms are arranged randomly, while glass atoms are ordered.

questions.s: Why does the author mention "the age of the universe"?
questions.e: The author says noticeable flow "would take far longer than the age of the universe," an extreme comparison showing that flow at room temperature is effectively impossible. This supports the rejection of the myth. Nothing in the passage says glass becomes more viscous with age.
o: To suggest that glass was first made very long ago
To compare the age of glass with the age of quartz
To show that glass gradually becomes far more viscous as it grows older
To stress how extremely slowly glass would flow, if at all

questions.s: What can be inferred about the old panes mentioned in paragraph 3?
questions.e: The passage says uneven panes "are better explained by older manufacturing methods, which rarely produced sheets of uniform thickness." So the panes were most likely uneven from the start. The last option depends on the flow myth that the passage rejects.
o: They were installed upside down by mistake.
They were probably uneven from the time they were made.
They are made of quartz rather than ordinary glass.
They will become thicker at the bottom over the next few centuries.

questions.s: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
questions.e: The passage defines the self-fulfilling prophecy, illustrates it with a bank run, and ends by saying the concept "remains valuable, though its power in any given setting should not be assumed." The correct option combines both points. Merton "built on" the Thomas theorem rather than rejecting it, and the bank run is a single imagined example, not a claim about most bank failures.
o: Bank failures are usually caused by rumors spread by depositors rather than by any real financial problems.
Beliefs can produce the outcomes they predict, though the size of the effect varies.
Teachers' expectations have been proven to determine students' intelligence.
Merton rejected the Thomas theorem and replaced it with a new theory.

questions.s: The word "replicate" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: "Attempts to replicate" the study produced their own results, which were compared with what was "first claimed," so researchers were doing the study again. Replicate means repeat. "Criticize" is tempting because criticism is mentioned in the same sentence, but it describes a separate response to the study.
o: publish
criticize
explain
repeat

questions.s: Why does the author describe a bank run in paragraph 2?
questions.e: The bank is "financially sound" until depositors act on a rumor, and the prediction "became true only because people acted on it." This is an example of a self-fulfilling prophecy. The third option reverses the passage, which says "no bank keeps all of its deposits as cash."
o: To illustrate how acting on a false belief can make it come true
To warn readers against keeping all of their savings in only one bank
To show that banks normally keep all deposits as cash
To explain why the Thomas theorem was first proposed

questions.s: What can be inferred about the bank in Merton's example?
questions.e: The bank was "financially sound until a rumor spreads," and "the rush itself" caused its failure. Without the rumor there would have been no rush, so it would likely have survived. The second option contradicts the statement that banks do not keep all deposits as cash, which is why the rush could ruin it.
o: It had already lost most of its deposits before the rumor.
It kept enough cash to repay every depositor at once.
It would probably have survived if the rumor had not spread.
It started the rumor in order to attract new depositors to it.

questions.s: Which of the following best describes the author's view of the self-fulfilling prophecy?
questions.e: The final sentence says the concept "remains valuable, though its power in any given setting should not be assumed," which means its strength must be checked in each case. The first option goes too far, because replications found effects that are "real but considerably smaller," not absent. The third option exaggerates the classroom findings.
o: It is an outdated idea that recent research has disproved.
It is a useful idea whose strength should be judged case by case.
It explains nearly all differences in student achievement.
It applies to financial behavior but never to classrooms.

questions.s: What is the main purpose of the passage?
questions.e: The passage challenges the image of Mozart receiving works "fully formed" by pointing to a forged letter and to surviving "sketches, drafts, and ... unfinished fragments." The correct option states this aim. The passage never ranks the two composers' talent, and it relies on sketches as evidence rather than dismissing them.
o: To show that Beethoven was a more talented composer than Mozart
To describe how Mozart's letters were collected and published
To question a popular image of Mozart using documentary evidence
To argue that sketches have little value for understanding a composer's work

questions.s: The word "painstaking" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: Beethoven's sketchbooks record "painstaking struggles over individual themes," meaning slow, effortful and careful work. "Very careful" fits. "Painful to hear" is a trap based on the first part of the word; the struggles were in the writing, not in the sound.
o: very careful
quick
painful to hear
unsuccessful

questions.s: What does the author suggest about why the image of Mozart as an effortless genius became popular?
questions.e: The author says the letter's appeal "may say more about the nineteenth century than about Mozart," since Romantic writers liked the idea of the artist as "a vessel for mysterious inspiration." So the image fit the tastes of that era. The fragments point the other way, showing that Mozart revised and abandoned work.
o: Mozart himself repeated the story in many later interviews.
Beethoven's sketchbooks were used to support it.
Scholars confirmed it by studying Mozart's unfinished fragments.
It suited ideas about artists that were fashionable in the nineteenth century.

questions.s: Why does the author include the sentence beginning "Admittedly, his memory and speed were extraordinary"?
questions.e: "Admittedly" signals a concession: the author grants that Mozart's abilities were exceptional. The next sentence, "Yet extraordinary fluency is not the same as effortlessness," then limits that point. The first option is wrong because the author keeps the claim about revision, and the third is too extreme, since no comparison with every other composer is made.
o: To withdraw the claim that Mozart revised his work
To concede a point to the popular view before qualifying it
To show that Mozart wrote faster than any other composer
To explain why so many of Mozart's fragments were left unfinished

questions.s: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about the difference between Mozart's and Beethoven's working methods?
questions.e: Because "many of Mozart's working papers were probably lost or discarded," the author says "the evidence itself may exaggerate the difference." So the real difference may be smaller than it looks. The last option reverses the facts: it was Beethoven who kept his sketches.
o: It has been measured precisely using their sketchbooks.
It proves Beethoven found composing more difficult.
It may be smaller than the surviving evidence suggests.
It disappeared once Beethoven's sketches were discarded.

questions.s: How is the passage organized?
questions.e: Paragraph 1 poses the puzzle of self-sacrifice, paragraph 2 presents kin selection, and paragraph 3 adds reciprocal altruism for cases "Kinship cannot explain." The correct option matches this. The second option is too strong: kin selection receives support and is only shown to be incomplete, not "entirely mistaken."
o: Two experiments are described, and their methods are compared.
A theory is presented and then shown to be entirely mistaken.
Several species are ranked according to how often their members help one another.
A puzzle is posed, and two explanations that address it are discussed.

questions.s: The word "persist" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: The question is how self-sacrifice could persist "if those who display it leave fewer offspring," that is, how it could survive over generations. "Continue to exist" fits. "Develop rapidly" adds the idea of speed, which the sentence does not contain.
o: disappear
develop rapidly
continue to exist
be noticed

questions.s: According to paragraph 2, when should helping be most common under the theory of kin selection?
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says helping should be most common "when the benefit to the recipient, weighted by how closely the two are related, exceeds the cost to the helper." The correct option paraphrases "weighted by" as "adjusted for kinship." Previous help describes reciprocal altruism in paragraph 3, not kin selection.
o: When the helper has no offspring of its own and is unlikely to produce any in the future
When the benefit to a relative, adjusted for kinship, is greater than the cost
When the recipient has previously helped the helper
When the helper and the recipient belong to different species

questions.s: Why does the author mention vampire bats?
questions.e: The bats appear right after "Kinship cannot explain everything," and some of the bats that receive blood "are unrelated." They are an example of helping that needs another explanation. The third option reverses their role, since they show help going to non-relatives.
o: To give an example of helping that kin selection alone does not explain
To show that ground squirrels are more generous than bats
To support Hamilton's view that animals direct their help only at close relatives
To describe how bats find their meals at night

questions.s: What can be inferred about a vampire bat that has never shared blood with its roost-mates?
questions.e: Bats "tend to share with individuals that have previously shared with them," so a bat that has never shared has not built up this exchange and may be helped less. The first option reverses this. Nothing in the passage links a bat's sharing record to its relatedness to the others.
o: It will receive more help than other bats.
It is probably closely related to every other bat in the roost.
It is unable to find meals on its own.
It may be less likely to receive blood when it needs it.

questions.s: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
questions.e: The passage describes the dominant "Clovis first" model, shows how Monte Verde made it "unravel," and introduces a coastal alternative. The correct option summarizes this shift. The third option is too strong: the coastal route is an idea that is still difficult to test, and Monte Verde shows only that people arrived early.
o: New evidence has challenged a long-accepted model of how the Americas were settled.
Clovis spear points were first made in South America and later carried north to New Mexico.
Monte Verde proves that people arrived in the Americas by boat.
Rising sea levels destroyed most evidence of the Clovis culture.

questions.s: The word "unravel" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: The model "began to unravel" when Monte Verde produced evidence older than Clovis, evidence that contradicted the model. To unravel here is to fall apart. "Be tested" is tempting, but the sentence describes the model failing, not simply being examined.
o: expand
fall apart
become popular
be tested

questions.s: What can be inferred from paragraph 2 about the first people to reach the Americas?
questions.e: Clovis sites date to "roughly 13,000 years ago," and Monte Verde predated Clovis "by more than a thousand years," so people were in southern Chile over 14,000 years ago and "must have entered the Americas earlier still." The last option conflicts with the claim that the corridor may not have supported travelers early enough.
o: They arrived only after the makers of Clovis points had settled the continent.
They lived only in southern Chile.
They entered the Americas more than fourteen thousand years ago.
They traveled through the inland corridor as soon as it opened.

questions.s: Why does the author mention that "sea levels have risen since the end of the last Ice Age"?
questions.e: The sentence begins "Testing this idea is difficult, however, because sea levels have risen," and adds that early coastal sites "now lie underwater." The rise in sea level explains why evidence for the coastal route is hard to find. The passage links boats to the coastal migrants, not to the Clovis hunters.
o: To explain why the ice-free corridor closed
To show that early people preferred to live far from the coast
To support the claim that Clovis people used boats
To explain why the coastal theory is hard to confirm

questions.s: According to the passage, all of the following were part of the "Clovis first" model EXCEPT
questions.e: Paragraph 1 says the model held that Clovis toolmakers were the first inhabitants, that they crossed "a land bridge from Siberia," and that they moved through "an ice-free corridor" between two ice sheets. The Pacific coast route is the "alternative" in paragraph 3 that replaced it, so it was not part of the model.
o: People traveled south along the Pacific coast by boat.
People crossed a land bridge from Siberia.
Clovis toolmakers were the first inhabitants.
Migrants moved south through an opening between two ice sheets.

questions.s: What is the passage mainly about?
questions.e: The passage says feathers 'predate flight by millions of years', then discusses what feathers were first for and how this affects the flight debate. The correct option sums up both effects. The first option reverses the evidence: the fossils come from species that 'could not plausibly have flown', and the passage never says either flight model has been abandoned.
o: How fossils from China showed that feathers first evolved to help small dinosaurs glide down from tall trees
How finding feathers on non-flying dinosaurs changed questions about feathers and flight
Why insulation is now accepted as the only original function of feathers
